title: Oscars: Iraq picks ‘No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman’ as Best Intl. Feature Contender
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 6, 2026 5:45am 'No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman' Courtesy of the Venice Film Festival Iraq has selected No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman from Norwegian-Kurdish director Halkawt Mustafa as its official submission for the 2027 Oscar race in the Best International Feature category. The film was the unanimous pick of Iraq’s official National Selection Committee for the Academy Awards , mandated by the state ministry of culture. The film follows Vyan, a Kurdish sniper who has survived war by suppressing her emotions. When she learns that her younger sister, missing since the ISIS assault in 2014, may still be alive, she returns to Mosul, determined to rescue her. Avan Jamal ( The Exam ) stars as Vyan, alongside Norwegian actor Thorbjørn Harr. The main cast also includes Kanar Sarchl and Kader Jalal. Related Stories Movies May el-Toukhy Takes 'Woman Unknown' to Venice: "I've Used Every Part of Me to Make This Film" Movies Wim Wenders on His 14-Year Journey Building Peter Zumthor Doc 'From Inside Out' Mustafa, who was born in Iraqi Kurdistan and fled to Norway as a child, said the film was inspired by his encounter with a female Peshmerga sniper during the 2014 frontline battles, as female Kurdish fighters countered Islamic State attacks. The director’s previous films include Hiding Saddam Hussein , a documentary about the farmer who hid the Iraqi dictator for 235 days in 2003, Iraq’s 2016 Oscar submission The Classic , and the 2015 documentary The Women ISIS Fears , which also looked at the world of female Kurdish fighters. No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman was filmed on location in Mosul. Hene Films produced the film in co-production with La Media and The Chimney Pot. True Colours is handling international sales. The film will have its world premiere out of competition at the Venice Film Festival on Monday. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences will announce the 15 films on the best international feature film shortlist on Dec. 15. The five nominees will be announced Jan. 21, 2027. The 99th Academy Awards ceremony will take place on March 14, 2027. THR

title: ‘Woman Unknown’ Director May el-Toukhy Talks the Torment of World War II ‘Horizontal Collaborators’ and Venice’s Female Director Snub: ‘It’s a Structural Problem’
full_text: Sep 6, 2026 5:03am PT ‘Woman Unknown’ Director May el-Toukhy Talks the Torment of World War II ‘Horizontal Collaborators’ and Venice’s Female Director Snub: ‘It’s a Structural Problem’ By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest ‘The Truffle Hunters’ Directors Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw Look for the Perfect Wine in ‘Burgundy’: ‘A Great Glass of Wine Changes How You Perceive the World’ 2 days ago ‘Everest: The Other Side’ Directors Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin Talk Grief, Loss and Their Most Personal Film Yet: ‘You Don’t Get to Choose Your Calling’ 2 days ago Director of Haugesund Closing Film ‘The Murder of Benjamin’ Says the Infamous Neo-Nazi Killing Was a ‘Wake-Up Call for the Whole Nation’ But ‘They Are Rising Again’ 1 week ago See All Jasper Spanning In “ Woman Unknown ,” May el-Toukhy takes a closer look at women accused of having relationships with German soldiers during World War II. “When we started to build a story about a ‘horizontal collaborator,’ we realized that, during and after the war, the female body became part of national identity. But in Denmark, it wasn’t really explored.” Initially, she wanted to make a film about the witch hunts after the Reformation in the 1500s. Related Stories Moonfish’ Director and Stars Lucy Liu and Morgan Spector Break Down Their Black-and-White Animated Film About Isolated Astronauts And Why It’s an Allegory for ‘The Current Human Condition’ Rubaiyat Hossain on Bodies, Beauty and Venice, Toronto and London-Bound 'The Difficult Bride,' Clip Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE) “It was difficult to relate to the perpetrators because many of them were just maniac. And I’m interested in ambiguity,” she says. Then, she came across an old newspaper photo of a woman with a swastika painted on her back. Popular on Variety “You can find very similar stories that are thousands of years old. The shaving of a woman’s hair or her public shaming for ‘sharing’ her body is a very old concept. Even today, it’s still happening in many armed conflicts.” Still, this suffering tends to be ignored by historians. The title of her film references that silence as well. “I was inspired by Belarusian writer Svetlana Alexievich who wrote ‘The Unwomanly Face of War.’ She gathered these testimonies from women who talked about having their periods in war zones, hiding in sheds, and giving birth. It’s rare to have such recollections of the female experience during or after the war,” says el-Toukhy. For Marie, a housemaid and a nanny, the future looks bright: she’s about to marry her wealthy employer. But in the weeks leading up to liberation in 1945, she must do her best to survive and ensure that her secrets don’t catch up with her. “Our main character wants to remain unknown, but we haven’t told stories about these women either. When you see their photographs in the archives, they’re often labeled ‘unknown woman.’ Also because people didn’t care.” Ironically enough, “Women Unknown” has already made headlines because of Venice’s decision to include only one female director in the main competition . The festival later added documentary “Naza,” co-directed by Rachel Szor. “Obviously, I’m delighted to have been invited to this historic festival. But I would have loved to be in the company of more female directors in the competition. I do believe it’s a structural problem,” notes el-Toukhy. “We discussed how the idea of publicly shaming women is an old concept. Not having enough films by women is also an issue that goes way back. It’s reflected in the budgets we work with and the talent that wants to be involved. Even journalists talk about male directors differently than they talk about women. I’ve never heard a female director called a ‘genius’ – and I read many articles about male geniuses.” What’s the solution? “Everyone has to chip in and be a part of it. I will now have a chance to discuss this issue through my film, which is rather aptly called ‘Woman Unknown’. I’m happy to do so, even though the circumstances surrounding me being in the main competition are what they are.” “We have a lot of work to do in order to change that.” May el-Toukhy is interested in new solutions. As previously announced by Variety , she’s also part of the new Dogma 25 movement. You can find the full manifesto here . “It’s always healthy to disrupt your process as a filmmaker,” she says. “Dogma 25 is very much about how we make films. Even though I heard many yeses while making this film, I still feel like I had to run much faster. That that kind of sprint doesn’t necessarily benefit the result.” She adds: “The way we have to work is almost unbearable. You finish a film and you’re completely stressed out and exhausted. I could make another big European arthouse drama in the future – I’m not saying goodbye to that format. I just think we really need to rethink the way we make movies.” As in her previous films, el-Toukhy doesn’t care much for typically likable protagonists. In “Queen of Hearts,” she followed a woman who seduced her teenage stepson. In “Woman Unknown,” Marie makes questionable choices as her carefully built facade threatens to collapse. “It would be a betrayal to my sisters around the world if I only portrayed women as saints. It’s important that we tell stories about complex women in a nuanced way, just as we do with male characters. That rings truer to life.” She wanted to stick to a female perspective throughout the story. “Early on, we made a rule that we would never reproduce the male experience of war. [Marie] goes out of the house, but the streets represent danger. People are celebrating and there’s euphoria, chaos and vigilantisms. Her safe space is at home, but then insecurity and danger move in. Suddenly, there’s no safe space anymore.” For the longest time, no one dared to criticize “the liberators” and their brutal methods. “It would have been harder to tell this story 25 years ago when those generations were still alive. Some audience members will still be shocked or angry because their grandfather was part of the resistance movement, which became very strong in Denmark right up to the liberation. But not everyone should have been a part of it.” “It’s important to have discussions about what actually happened so that we don’t recreate false narratives. title: ‘From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor’ Review: Wim Wenders’ Latest 3D Documentary Is an Architectural Marvel
full_text: Sep 6, 2026 5:00am PT ‘From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor’ Review: Wim Wenders’ Latest 3D Documentary Is an Architectural Marvel The German filmmaker trains his stereoscopic lens on the buildings of the Swiss architect, revealing them in surprising ways. By Siddhant Adlakha Plus Icon Siddhant Adlakha Latest ‘Our Share of Sand’ Review: A Brooding Indian Social Drama Told Through the Eyes of a Young Girl 1 day ago ‘My Notes on Mars’ Review: Mackenzie Davis and Rupert Friend Star in an Imperfect Breakdown of Marriage and Memory 4 days ago ‘Onslaught’ Review: Adria Arjona and Dan Stevens Star in Adam Wingard’s Fun but Scattered Military Slasher 6 days ago See All Courtesy of Venice Film Festival The screen is usually a canvas, but it becomes a window to an enormous room in Wim Wenders ’ latest 3D documentary, “From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor.” Within that room unfolds the tale of the Swiss architect of the title, told in occasionally laborious ways. It spends much of its two-hour runtime teaching you how to watch it, and like your average high school class, you might not see the value of its instruction until it eventually comes in handy. In that vein, Wenders presents some magnificent things in the film’s final third, sensations which emerge like Zumthor’s own views on the function of his buildings, which he ties to human experience, understood by its inhabitants gradually, and then all at once — from the inside out. Related Stories 'The Echo Chamber' Starring Alicia Vikander Seals International Distribution Deals Ahead of Venice Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) Édgar Ramírez and Nahuel Pérez Biscayart to Star in ‘Land of the Savages’ by Venice-Winning ‘Blanquita’ Director Fernando Guzzoni Beginning with shots of concave corners and convex, monolithic surfaces, “From Inside Out” engenders curiosity before taking academic detours. These come courtesy of Zumthor himself, whom we first meet as a ghostly projection upon sleek, minimalist surfaces, emanating from the 1980s. Like the Holocaust survivors whose poetry populated the walls in Wenders’ “Anselm” — his 3D retrospective on the works of sculptor Anselm Kiefer — Zumthor’s words become inseparable from each room the camera explores, and each building the architect believes ought to feel at one with its surroundings. Popular on Variety We eventually meet Zumthor in the present: an unassuming man in his eighties, whose descriptions of form, function and fluidity often repeat themselves, but whose sincerity and wisdom are hard to shake. As the film explores houses, museums and other Zumthor commissions, the architect’s use of light and natural materials becomes as important as the theoretical people he intends to fill each space — or, in the case of complicated restorations, the people who inhabited them decades ago. Wenders depicts these ghosts of past and future through dramatizations of curious travelers, whose whispering voiceover offers scattered thoughts on where they stand. There’s a tinge of humor, too, in Zumthor’s stubbornness when designing someone’s home, as the conceptual clashes with the preferential. However, the architect eventually gives way to use and function first, despite valuing the aesthetics at hand (not to mention, his collaborations with local artisans). It isn’t long before Wenders introduces the idea that Zumthor’s spaces are only as important as what goes inside them, when he first contrasts old and contemporary footage of museums he designed, each filled with deeply personal art installations — some of them about war. Zumthor himself doesn’t have the most interesting personal history — at least, not as far as this film is concerned — so Wenders’ exploration can come off as superficial at first. However, this ends up part and parcel of the structure. It echoes the feeling of approaching a marvelous building from afar, and entering its sterile lobby, before slowly discovering its mischievous secrets. Although some scenes and enactments can meander, they give way to a moving triptych of projects whose presentation feels, in a way, climactic. One is a home deeply personal to Zumthor. Another is a Nordic installation built in tribute to women killed in witch trials, which feels terrifying to walk through — a kind of infinitude accentuated by Franz Lustig’s 3D cinematography. And the third is arguably Zumthor’s magnum opus: his sprawling, amoebic construction housing the permanent collection at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, whose planning and completion the doc depicts in detail. By the time the building is finished (and visited by a number of filmmakers, including Ava DuVernay and Werner Herzog), Wenders’ camera moves in tandem with Zumthor’s own abstract notions of the art pieces needing to feel horizontally equal, with none being granted more or less importance than any other. The sprawling gallery seems to have no beginning or end. Its bends extend endlessly, revealing pockets and side rooms with rough, exposed concrete contrasting the gilded grandeur of the pieces on display. It takes a while to realize this, or at least to internalize it, but the film’s own architecture is not dissimilar, with what feels like winding segues that add up to an experience of fluid expanse, of great wandering, and ultimately, of soulful appreciation. Certainly, no one is beholden to a film this demanding, but Wenders wields his 3D camera to craft a perfect marriage of subject and form, filling echoing spaces with art and stories much like Zumthor’s architecture does — until eventually, you leave with a new appreciation of the physical world, and your place within it. ‘From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor’ Review: Wim Wenders’ Latest 3D Documentary Is an Architectural Marvel Reviewed at Venice Film Festival (Out of Competition), Sept. 5, 2026. title: Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers’ Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: ‘We Are the Opposite of Politicians … We Are the Antidote’
full_text: Sep 6, 2026 3:44am PT Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers’ Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: ‘We Are the Opposite of Politicians … We Are the Antidote’ By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers’ Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: ‘We Are the Opposite of Politicians … We Are the Antidote’ 2 hours ago Liam and Noel Gallagher Raise Fists and Electrify Venice as Oasis Doc Gets 8-Minute Standing Ovation 14 hours ago Liam and Noel Gallagher Skip Oasis Documentary Press Conference at Venice Film Festival 23 hours ago See All Getty Images Wim Wenders has clarified his much-discussed statement about filmmakers’ role in politics that kicked off a firestorm at Berlin Film Festival earlier this year. Wenders was at the center of a heated debate at the Berlinale in February after the celebrated German filmmaker, who served as jury president, said during the opening press conference that filmmakers “ should stay out of politics .” Related Stories Robert Pattinson Wants Chris Hansen to Like 'Primetime' Despite His Criticisms: 'I Hope the Inspiration His Character Has Given Is Some Kind of Compliment' 'Pamfir' Helmer Dmytro Sukholytkyy-Sobchuk Realized His Kyiv Apartment ‘Could Be Bombed Any Day,’ So He Remortgaged It to Fund ‘Something Strange Happened to Me’ “We have to stay out of politics because if we make movies that are dedicatedly political, we enter the field of politics,” Wenders said at the time. “But we are the counterweight of politics, we are the opposite of politics. We have to do the work of people, not the work of politicians.” Popular on Variety The statement then dominated the discourse at the festival, with nearly every filmmaker and actor facing a question about politics — including the ongoing conflict in Gaza and ICE raids in the U.S. — during their respective press conferences. Author Arundhati Roy even pulled out of the festival in protest, and festival director Tricia Tuttle had to put out a statement in response to the frenzy. Asked to reflect on his statement Sunday during a press conference at Venice Film Festival , where he is presenting his latest documentary “From Inside Out — The Architecture of Peter Zumthor,” Wenders said that he “could repeat the same thing,” though admitted he “could be more explicit.” “What I said then was, as filmmakers, we are the opposite of politicians. We have empathy. Politics work without empathy; that’s all I said,” Wenders, who sported an “Imagine Peace” shirt, began. “We have a very different thing. I’m not working with a mindset of politicians, we are working with a mindset of empathetic people. And we are into changing things, politics are into confirming what is.” He continued, “That’s what I said and was quoted as ‘We have to stay out of politics,’ and that is not what I said, because it’s not what I said now and I said the same thing then. The frame of filmmakers is a different mindset than the mindset of politicians, and we should not work with that mindset. We work with a different set of rules. I said it again, and I hope you’re not misquoting me and say we have to stay out of politics, because we do the opposite. We are the antidote.” At Venice’s opening press conference earlier in the festival, jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal weighed in on the topic, saying that movies are “fundamentally, undeniably political.” “Look, we could say, how are we possibly here talking about movies right now when the world is in a state of emergency?” she said. “To me, the answer has something to do with empathy. full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Emmy Awards Night 1 Winners: The Full List Read the full story By Damon Wise Damon Wise Film Editor, Awards yo_damo More Stories By Damon ‘Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger’ Review: The Gallagher Bros. Bury The Hatchet In A Sentimental But Funny Concert Movie – Venice Film Festival ‘Primetime’ Review: Robert Pattinson Channels Jerry Maguire And Dracula For Lance Oppenheim’s Dark TV Morality Tale – Venice Film Festival Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews View All September 6, 2026 3:20am 'Father Joe' Venice Film Festival Did you ever feel that King of New York could have done with a bit more Wing Chun? Did you ever think that John Woo’s films weren’t quite Catholic enough? That the siege of Troy might have been handled a bit more successfully if the Greeks had a bazooka? If your answer is yes to even one of these questions, then Barthélémy Grossmann’s old-school beat-’em-is for you, a violent multifaith mob movie with a script so fantastically absurd it can only come from the mind of French auteur Luc Besson , who somehow segued from Le Cinema du Look of the ’80s to Le Cinema du Kaboom of the ’90s. It’s been 32 years since Besson unveiled his international breakout hit Léon , but it’s yesterday once more in Father Joe , which begins in uptown New York, sometime in the pre-internet ’90s, with the unmistakable sounds of the Notorious B.I.G. blasting out on the radio of a blinged-out town car. Veteran gangster Lino ( Michael Rispoli ) is taking his trophy girlfriend into the depths of a desolate industrial estate, where bored lackeys with guns and gold chains keep watch. “People would kill to know about this place,” he says, which isn’t quite the flex he thinks it is, and his date is right to be nervous. Related Stories News Danny Boyle Confirms Use Of AI In New Movie 'Ink' News 'Father Joe': First Look Clip Of Kiefer Sutherland As A Priest Who Clashes With The Mob In Action-Crime Pic -- Venice “This place” is a drug lab, and while Lino is checking out his investment, a man in black starts picking of his crew with the stealth of a ninja and the armory of the Marine Corp. After shooting Lino in the foot, the stranger reveals himself as Father Joe ( Kiefer Sutherland ), an actual priest who takes on Manhattan’s drug dealers wearing his work clothes. “I’m here to put you back on the right track,” he says, and orders him to confess. Watch on Deadline Being a good Catholic boy, as all mobsters used to be, Lino does so, and Father Joe lets him live on two conditions: One, no selling drugs to kids under the age of 21. “You can’t save everyone,” he reasons, with a strangely beatific smile. The other condition is way more Bessonian: Father Joe injects Lino with a complex homemade virus that will become deadly within seven days. To stay alive, Lino must attend Communion every week at Father Joe’s Church on 118 th Street, where he will be given a temporary antidote. But when Lino arrives at the church, he is surprised to see a number of other wiseguys, who line up to take a little blue pill while everyone else gets a wafer. Father Joe’s operation, which is decimating the local drug trade, is hardly undercover (unless you count the secret arms chamber behind a statue of the Virgin Mary), and pretty soon it comes to the attention of crime boss Giu ( Al Pacino ), who has noticed a dip in takings lately. Giu pays Father Joe a visit and gets infected with the same virus after being lured into the confession box. Giu, however, is not as gullible as the men who work for him and gets himself to the hospital for a thorough medical. While Giu is doing this, the story shifts up a gear. Vulnerable local children have started going missing, which may or may not have something to do with a privately run hospital, where rich parents pay through the nose for organ transplants of a very dubious provenance. This sudden shift from drugs to body parts suggests that Father Joe may have been intended as a mini-series (or at the very least a comic book), having the freewheeling quality of ’the ’70s TV show Kung Fu . Father Joe himself certainly has the backstory for it, being a war veteran who married an Asian woman who died young and lost his grieving daughter to an overdose. This not only explains Father Joe’s benevolence, it also opens up room for a sassy sidekick: 16-year-old drug casualty Felicity, who’s played by Ever Anderson, daughter of The Fifth Element star Milla Jovovich. A child from a broken home, Felicity soon goes native and wants in on Father Joe’s set-up, much to his horror. Despite this strange digression, Besson’s script soon gets back on track when Giu gets the results of his tests back and declares war on Father Joe. And this does mean war; Grossmann’s deliriously violent actioner commands an insane amount of firepower but still finds time for some classic throwbacks — such as a fantastically staged fist fight in an elevator — while the body count climbs into the heights of a Takeshi Miike movie. Amazingly, Al Pacino is about the only thing that isn’t over the top here, generously giving center stage to Keifer Sutherland in a role that’s fun, unbelievable — and sometimes unbelievably funny (wait for the cardinal to deliver the punchline) — but, like Besson’s 2023 film Dogman , it’s never laughable, such is everyone’s commitment. Is it any good? Who knows. It’s certainly the most balls-out, no-f*cks-given rock’n’roll phenomenon to hit the Lido this year — and that includes the Gallagher brothers. title: Richard Osman Appears To Confirm ‘The Celebrity Traitors’ Premiere Date Amid Talk That Season 2 Was “Intense” To Film

View All September 6, 2026 2:58am Richard Osman and 'The Celebrity Traitors' Getty/BBC Richard Osman has apparently let slip that The Celebrity Traitors will return to the BBC this month. Speaking on-stage during a live episode of The Rest Is Entertainment podcast in London, Osman told the audience that The Celebrity Traitors will premiere on September 23. Osman and co-host Marina Hyde were interviewing special guest Joe Marler, the former England rugby player who has become a fixture on UK television since appearing in Season 1 of The Celebrity Traitors . Per a Press Association report, Marler was asked what advice he would give contestants when he speculated on Season 2’s premiere date: “What is it, September 23, the next series?” Related Stories Legal Lindsay Clancy Mistrial: Jury Deadlock Proves Too Much To Continue Triple-Murder Case, For Now News BBC Board Members Told To Seek Legal Advice Before Traveling To U.S. Amid Trump Lawsuit Osman chimed in: “By the way, to point out, it’s absolutely embargoed that it starts on September 23 … let’s talk about what we call the events of September 23 this year … the cat’s out of the bag, isn’t it? Not to repeat it.” Watch on Deadline A BBC insider joked that they did not realize Marler was “moonlighting in the BBC One scheduling team,” but declined to confirm that September 23 was the premiere date. During the conversation at London’s Southbank Centre on Saturday, Osman said he had heard from Season 2 celebrities that it “was quite intense” to film. Deadline has also heard chatter about Season 2, with one well-placed source describing it as a “nightmare” that was tricky for producers Studio Lambert. Marler shed a little more light. He told Osman and Hyde: “I believe it was a slightly different emotion than our experience. Ours was very laugh-led, and everyone was sort of enjoying catching up, you know, pratting about to the point where they [the producers] went: ‘Guys, we’re trying to play a game.’ He continued: “Whereas this lot really want it from the start, and then I guess they see how well the first series has gone and there’s a little bit of pressure on them to be like: ‘Oh, I’d quite like a bit of that.’” Speaking at the Edinburgh TV Festival last month, BBC content chief Kate Phillips revealed that there will be tears and surprises in the new season, hosted by Claudia Winkleman. The show will feature an eye-catching cast including The Last of Us star Bella Ramsey , Good Omens actor Michael Sheen , and Oscar-nominated Richard E. Grant . Others include Industry star Myha’la, Barbie actress Sharon Rooney, Love Island host Maya Jama, Broadchurch’s Julie Hesmondhalgh, and Jerry Hall, the model and actress who was married to Mick Jagger. Season 1 of The Celebrity Traitors was the most-watched show on British TV last year. It debuted on BBC iPlayer and BBC One in October 2025 and was seen by an average audience of 14.9M, with a peak of 15.4M for the finale. Comedian Alan Carr emerged victorious in a game that featured Stephen Fry and Celia Imrie. The Celebrity Traitors is produced by Studio Lambert Scotland for BBC One and iPlayer and has been commissioned by Kalpna Patel-Knight, Head of Entertainment Commissioning for the BBC. The executive producers for All3Media-backed Studio Lambert are Mike Cotton, Sarah Fay, Lewis Thurlow and Katy Fox, with production executives, Lynette Woods-Reynolds, Gemma Scholes and Faye Donaldson. The commissioning editors for the BBC are Neil McCallum and Michael Jochnowitz. The Traitors (Dutch title: De Verraders ) was created and developed by IDTV in cooperation with RTL Creative Unit. title: French President Emmanuel Macron Calls for a ‘New Multilateralism’ Across Creative Industries: ‘We Built a Civilization of Images. We Should Not Resign Ourselves to Watching It Deteriorate’
full_text: Sep 6, 2026 2:30am PT French President Emmanuel Macron Calls for a ‘New Multilateralism’ Across Creative Industries: ‘We Built a Civilization of Images. We Should Not Resign Ourselves to Watching It Deteriorate’ The op-ed comes on the eve of the Lumière Summit, which Macron is co-hosting with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung to bring together global entertainment leaders around the future of cinema, TV and gaming By Emmanuel Macron Plus Icon Emmanuel Macron Latest See All DR In 1895, the first public film screening happened. It was in the basement of the Grand Café, nearby the Paris Opera, with a program of 10 short movies, each no more than 50 seconds long. Cinema was born. The names of the two brothers, Auguste and Louis Lumière, became symbols of an art which needs darkness to make light happens. It heralded a new era of our long-standing Civilization of Images. More than a century after, movies and, more broadly, the moving image industry including video games and animation, are more than ever part of our daily lives. From movie theaters, moving images traveled to the television screens and personal devices and, over the past deeply transformative decade, they have found their way into the palms of our hands. One cannot think about visual culture without thinking about screens. Related Stories Al Pacino Sends Video Message to Venice After Missing Press Conference for 'Father Joe': 'I Wish I Was There, I Really Do' 'The Echo Chamber' Starring Alicia Vikander Seals International Distribution Deals Ahead of Venice Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) Screens, in themselves, are neutral. They can be an opportunity to get closer to any audience or a source of risk as we all know from the rise of social media and the inflation of images that some have described as a form of cognitive war. Popular on Variety We see the effects everywhere. Parents worry about their children’s attention. Teachers compete with a permanent flow of images. Artists wonder whether their work can still find an audience. Governments debate technologies that evolve faster than legislation. And each of us knows the strange experience of reaching for a screen for one reason and emerging much later, having forgotten why. Yet the screen itself is not our enemy. It has brought extraordinary things into our lives. Never before have so many people had access to so many films, ideas and cultures other than their own. It’s clear to all of us that a screen can educate, connect and inspire. The question is how to preserve that promise while confronting what has gone wrong. We should begin by acknowledging something uncomfortable: we shaped this world, and we must take responsibility for it. But because we shaped it, we can reshape it. The remedy is not to turn away from screens. It is to change our relationship with them on the screens themselves. To remain lucid about the ways our relationship with screens can damage our world, while being ambitious enough to fulfill their promise, we should look to the arts of the moving image: cinema, series and video games. They have been transformed by the digital revolution. But they also show us what a screen can offer at its best: sustained attention, imagination, authorship and a shared experience of another world. Here is the paradox. We have never spent so much time in front of screens, and never so little time with the works that these screens were built to carry. Yet those works contain much of what made the moving image so transformative in the first place. A film can send a new generation back to Homer. A series rooted in one language and one place can become a global conversation. A video game can ask us not merely to watch a world, but to inhabit it. One distinction therefore matters: the difference between an endless supply of content and works that require time, talent, risk and intention to create. The value of these works is economic. If the screen industries lose the capacity to finance ambitious works, take risks on unfamiliar voices or sustain the institutions that bring them to audiences, the consequences will eventually show up on our screens. There may be more images than ever, and fewer genuinely different things to see. Their value is also cultural. Works preserve memory, give form to experience and allow one society to enter the imagination of another. They allow cultures to recognize themselves and to discover one another. And their value is democratic. A society in which everyone is shown what an algorithm predicts will hold their attention is not quite the same society as one in which citizens still encounter stories, ideas and lives they did not choose in advance. When the systems that shape our attention are optimized above all for engagement, we should not be surprised if public conversation itself becomes shorter, angrier and more fragmented. The value we give to creative works is therefore not only an economic question for the future of the screen industries. It is a cultural and democratic question for the future of our societies. This is why the moment matters. Several transformations are now happening at once: the fragmentation of attention, the concentration of the channels through which works reach audiences, profound changes in how creation is financed, new forms of production and distribution, and the rapid rise of generative artificial intelligence. Taken separately, each might look like one more disruption an industry will adapt to. Taken together, they are changing the conditions in which images are created, financed, distributed and seen. We should not wait until this new order has become permanent and only then describe it as inevitable. Responding requires a method. No single company and no single nation, however large, can find the solution alone. What we need is a new form of cooperation: a new multilateralism for the moving image, pursued with the same seriousness we have brought to trade, climate and security. That does not mean building a global bureaucracy for culture. It means bringing to the same table actors who too rarely address these questions together: governments, creators, studios, producers, broadcasters, platforms, cinemas and public institutions. Governments do not make films. Artists do not design the technologies through which billions encounter them. Companies cannot define the public interest on their own. And no national institution can respond alone to forces that cross borders by design: technologies, capital, works and audiences. The purpose of this dialogue should not be to defend yesterday’s model. It should be to build the conditions for a richer creative future: to preserve the possibility of creating ambitious works, ensure that they can circulate, give audiences the tools to navigate an age of infinite images, and make technological progress compatible with human creativity. This conversation must be global. That is why, this September, together with the President of the Republic of Korea, I will convene the Lumière Summit. France and South Korea have taken different paths, but both have shown that openness to the world can strengthen, rather than erase, a distinctive creative culture. Governments, artists, companies and institutions will come together to begin building a common response, and to move beyond the divisions of yesterday. For this moment also offers a rare opportunity for convergence: between cinema, television and gaming; between public authorities and private companies; and between regions of the world that have too often approached these challenges separately. The transformations affecting us are shared. Our response should be as well. The United States has shaped an extraordinary part of the history and imagination of the moving image, and its leadership will remain essential to what comes next. Asia has become one of the industry’s greatest creative centers. Across Africa, new generations of storytellers are meeting some of the world’s fastest-growing audiences. The Middle East is home to some of contemporary cinema’s most vital voices. Latin America has repeatedly shown how stories deeply rooted in one place can speak to the world. Europe brings its own experience: decades of showing that creative industries can be open to the world without losing their roots, and that economic ambition, technological innovation and cultural sovereignty can strengthen one another. France carries a particular responsibility in this conversation. Proud that cinema was born in France 130 years ago, we should not seek to preserve it in amber. Our task is to help create the conditions in which it can be reinvented. We built a civilization of images. We should not resign ourselves to watching it deteriorate. The same screens that have become part of the problem can also carry the solution: greater access, greater choice, new forms of creation, new encounters between cultures. The task is not to turn back. It is to decide, together, what kind of civilization of images we want to build — and whether we have the ambition to make moving images one of the most valuable Common Goods of our times. title: Wim Wenders on His 14-Year Journey Building Peter Zumthor Doc ‘From Inside Out’
full_text: × Skip to main content 'From Inside Out: The Architecture of Peter Zumthor' Road Movies Wim Wenders has spent much of the past three decades building portraits of other artists — the Cuban musicians of Buena Vista Social Club (1999), the choreographer Pina Bausch in Pina (2011) , the photographer Sebastião Salgado in The Salt of the Earth (2014), the German painter-sculptor Anselm Kiefer in Anslem (2023) . The first three were Oscar-nominated. All were critically acclaimed. But none has taken him as long as From Inside Out: The Architecture of Peter Zumthor , the German auteur’s 3D documentary on the Pritzker Prize-winning Swiss architect, has been 14 years in the making. Related Stories Movies May el-Toukhy Takes 'Woman Unknown' to Venice: "I've Used Every Part of Me to Make This Film" Movies Liam and Noel Gallagher Lock Arms at Venice Premiere of 'Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger' It started small. David Chipperfield, curating the 2012 Venice architecture Biennale, asked Wenders to make a short film on Zumthor. That became a two-day shoot in the architect’s modest office in Haldenstein, high in the Swiss mountains, and the 2012 short Notes on a Day in the Life of an Architect — along with the nagging sense that he had barely scratched the surface. “At the end, we shook hands on ‘doing something real together,'” Wenders says. “Little did we know that the journey would last 14 years…” The result, premiering in Venice, and being sold worldwide by HanWay Films, is a two-hour immersion that wanders from some of Zumthor’s earliest works, including the St. Benedict’s chapel, completed in 1988, to a memorial for burned witches above the Arctic Circle, to the newly opened $724 million David Geffen Galleries at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA), the architect’s largest building, commissioned nearly two decades ago. [Brad Pitt, a fan of Zumthor, who supported his LACMA bid, has joined From Inside Out as an executive producer. ] Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter ahead of the premiere, Wenders discussed his kinship with Zumthor, why he needed 3D to shoot architecture, what a craftsman’s hands can teach the age of AI, and how he answers the charge that Zumthor’s serene spaces are a luxury in a world of flattened cities. “Buildings cannot repair the world,” he says. “But they can change our idea of what the world could be.” How did you first come to know Peter Zumthor? How did the idea for this film come about? I was invited to make a short film on Peter Zumthor for the architectural Biennale in Venice in 2012, by none other than British architect David Chipperfield, who was the curator of the show that year. I knew some of Zumthor’s buildings, and I was intrigued by the idea. It became a 2-day shoot in his office in Haldenstein, way up in the Swiss mountains, and resulted in Notes on a Day in the Life of an Architect , but also in the realization that this short study just scratched the surface of Zumthor’s work, his philosophy and his approach. At the end, we shook hands on ‘doing something real together’, and that was clearly going to be a long-term observation. Little did we know that the journey would last 14 years… What is it about his work that is distinctive and particularly compelling for you? Peter Zumthor had a relatively small office, and he did not want to change that. He wanted to be able to keep accepting only work that he was absolutely convinced of, of its purpose, of its necessity, of its usefulness and its site. He doesn’t want to be just a hired architect. He wants to be thoroughly involved and make the best possible building for that particular use and at that particular place. And for that, he knows he needs more time than is usually given to develop a building. But most of all: he wants the client to understand that once he proposes a design, he is not going to step away from the project. Like a painter, he knows that his painting will only emerge in the act of painting it. A songwriter or a poet works the same way: the song and the poem are only finished after the last act of correction. And that is exactly the freedom that architects are usually not given in the building process. A construction company takes over. The architect cannot intervene anymore, at least not with important changes. That understanding of the creative process is what I can deeply identify with. He is convinced that a work is not finished when it is planned, but that it continues to take shape in the making. I feel exactly the same way about filmmaking. For me, too, a film is not basically done with the script. I want to be able to change that script, as I go along. I even want to be able to contradict it. THAT is the act of creation: having the liberty to continue learning about how your story will turn out best. That is the very nature of storytelling: finding out the truth of your story as you’re telling it. Peter Zumthor is asking for exactly that freedom that I also fight for with every film: invent and improve the film – or the building – as you are making it. Why did you want to film this in 3D? When I made my first film in 3D, Pina , on the art of choreographer Pina Bausch, 3D was the saving grace of that project. I would not have made it if the new medium hadn’t allowed me to work in the same realm as Pina and her dancers. And that was SPACE . A screen is a two-dimensional thing, any effort to represent space on it is make-believe. Cinema has been incredibly inventive in this make-believe and has invented many tools to convince the audience that the story they were watching was taking place inside space, even if the movies were always a medium restricted to the flat screen. Only the invention of digital 3D, native 3D, has made the screen go away and become a window, open to infinity and also to things taking place in front of the window. From Inside Out is my tenth film in 3D, short ones and installations included. But it was never more necessary (after Pina ) than now. A ‘room’ and a ‘house’ belong to our earliest human experiences and they mean ‘shelter’, ‘protection’ and ‘security’. These are not abstract ideas at first, they are spatial experiences, utterly existential. We experience space before we learn about its abstraction, the two-dimensional representation of it, in photos, in drawings, in paintings, on TV or in the cinema. Architecture is the one art, together with dance and theatre, that is unthinkable without space. So if I wanted an audience to experience the world of an architect, I felt I needed space itself at my disposal, not just as a technology, but as a cinematic language. Parts of the film have the feel of an art or museum installation. Do you envision the project living on in those spaces? No. I make it for movie theatres. But I take your question as a compliment. You certainly have different experiences in museums than in movies. I feel it is time to expand the limits of what we can experience in movie theatres. Poster for ‘From Inside Out: The Architecture of Peter Zumthor’ Courtesy of HanWay Films You take different approaches in depicting Zumthor’s work — interviews with the family for the Luzi house, with voice-over commentary from other artists, as a stage for dance or musical performance — what was behind this and, in the case of collaborations with other artists — Aoi Yamada, Siri Hustvedt, Sophie Hunger, etc. — how did those come about? I didn’t want to make a ‘talking heads’ film. I didn’t want to make a didactic film, period. I wanted the audience to experience architecture without having to verbalize the issues all the time, like a TV documentary. Houses give us an immense freedom to explore them: we can walk around in them, sit down and look out of a window, work or sleep or dream in them. They get under our skin. We find out how we live in them, think in them, ARE in them. Some chapters in From Inside Out are strictly based on the audience sharing the experience of some of my protagonists in being in the buildings of Peter Zumthor. Siri Hustvedt, for instance, had written about the women who were burned as witches in that part of Norway, far above the Arctic Circle. But she had never seen the place Zumthor built in memory of these women. Her experience of encountering that building becomes the film in that chapter. Who can travel so far north – further north than any city in the US or Canada – to visit this one-of-a-kind place and this absolutely unique building that is like nothing that was ever built before? Well, not many. But you can almost physically enter the building in the film… What was behind your musical choices for each building – both the live performances and the accompanying score? The score is made almost equally by two very different voices: one is Peter Zumthor’s son Peter Conradin Zumthor as percussionist together with his partner, pianist Vera Kappeler. The other is my long-trusted composer friend Laurent Petitgand with whom I made more than a dozen films in the past. These two ‘voices’ serve two very different aspects of Zumthor’s world. The percussion as well as the piano, I felt, both have a great affinity to more structural aspects of space and time, while the more symphonic music has a great affinity to the emotional aspects of the work. The two live performances come from an altogether different thinking. The amazing St. Benedict’s chapel that Zumthor built as a young architect reminded me very much of a musical instrument. Visiting it, I felt I was entering the body of a cello or a bigger string instrument. So in order to explore it, I invited a double bass player, Anna Trauffer, to join us and play in the chapel. And as she also sings and plays musical glasses, we could also hear a beautiful human voice inside this ‘instrument’ called ‘a chapel’ as well as her glass harp. For Zumthor’s latest building, the extension of the Beyeler Foundation in Basel, now called the Wyss Building, I had the idea of inviting the great Sophie Hunger, one of my favorite contemporary singer-songwriters, to visit the new (and yet not quite finished) building and walk the path that Peter Zumthor invented for this building, from one outlook into the surrounding landscape to another. I admit, that was just a vague idea, at first, also the fact that she might invent a song for this ‘walk with a guitar’ that could somehow condense or tie together some of Peter Zumthor’s ‘philosophy’ or ‘approach’. Little did I know how masterful she would combine these two tasks and come up with her song From Inside to Outside, that in the end even reflects the film’s title. Both musical performances, I felt, were gifts to our film. What connections do you see between the work of the architect and that of the filmmaker? I could talk about that issue for an entire hour or more. But just let me say this: as a filmmaker, I construct a movie from pieces of time. Every shot is such a ‘brick of time’. Every scene is a ‘room’ or a ‘space’ made from such tiny elements of time. And the entire film, in the end, is a huge building or ‘space’ constructed from many such bricks of time. Editing a film is a building process. In the end, the film invites people to live in its space, at least for a couple of hours. I better stop here, before I get carried away… Are you spiritual kin to Peter Zumthor, do you see yourself as struggling with similar questions and themes, and pursuing similar aims? There is one thing we definitely share, as a passion, or as an approach, or an aim. (And yes, we might “struggle” with lots of questions and problems while making a movie or conceiving a building. But I don’t make films to have anybody watch me ‘struggle’, let alone my actors. People want to see Odysseus struggle, not Matt Damon, nor Christopher Nolan. And I assume Peter doesn’t want his buildings to show any traces of him having ‘struggled’ with them before, either…) Let’s say we know and love the processes that go with our professions, but we are both particularly fond of the fact that our work is concerned with PLACES . For Zumthor, every building is planted onto a particular site which has its history, its surroundings, its nature, its weather, its neighbors, in short: its geographic conditions. He wants to do justice to them. More so: he wants his new building to belong there, “as if it had always been there.” (to quote him.) He wants the building to live in peace with its neighbors and its nature. So he has to find out a lot about the place, before he could even consider designing something for it. He first has to read the place, understand it and grasp what the place needs as an addition, as a new neighbor, possibly a new center of attention. And he has to fully transcend the purpose of the building to make it go in unison with the place, not against it. So, what is really demanded from an architect is A SENSE OF PLACE . It’s one of our original human senses, even if most of us don’t use it much anymore. We have delegated it to our navigation systems. As a filmmaker, I equally depend on my sense of place. Most of my films, if not all, don’t start with ‘story’, but with a place, a place that I encounter and respond to emotionally. I then want to find a story that could happen here, more so: that could only play here, in that place. My films are all ‘taking place’ on these crossroads of a place and a story that belong together. What does Peter Zumthor and the method of his art have to teach our modern age, the age of AI? His buildings are deeply human, the result of a long dialogue between the site (its surrounding nature or city landscape) and the purpose of the new building. Zumthor thinks it from the inside first, the new space he’s about to conceive, then considers it from outside, which might lead to corrections, then sees what this does to the perspective from inside, then returns to seeing it from the outside. That dialogue does take time and includes his collaborators, the client and endless sessions in his office. In that process, countless models are being built and rebuilt and discarded and started from scratch again. The buildings that are thus given time to grow and develop, find their affinity to the site in that long dialogue, find their materiality and also sometimes redefine their purpose. It’s like a gardening process, I sometimes felt when I returned to Peter and the building I saw months before now had not only ‘grown’, but assumed more character, as if it had ascertained its identity. That’s why they are so totally unique. About some of them, like the Witches Memorial way up North in the Arctic or the David Geffen Galleries of the LACMA in California, one can safely say there is no other building on the planet like it. All of Zumthor’s buildings can open our eyes to what architecture can be and what it can do to expand our understanding of spaces and places. I’m not sure how many years we are away from AI learning to design buildings. Let alone replace the touch of human hands involved in the building process. Zumthor’s big message in the film is: learn to see the beauty of things made by hand, by craftspeople! We must not lose that! (laughs) At this moment, I’m sure AI can only learn from our man. (Or other architects and artists. Asked if AI can write a good song, Nick Cave answered: “I don’t think so. AI can’t suffer.”) There are a couple of moments in the film where Zumthor connects his work with his personal experience of wanting to create homes, a secure space to compensate for not feeling safe as a child. But you avoid going very deep into a psychological exploration of him or his biography. Why that choice? You’re right: it was a choice. I did not want to shoot a biopic on an architect. This film is not about how Peter Zumthor became who he is. It is not about his life, but how his ideas took shape and how they’re connecting to the feelings or to the curiosity the audience might have about architecture. We all live and work and die in houses, we grow up and get old in schools, offices, museums, churches or whatever buildings we visit. But doing so, we mostly take architecture for granted. From Inside Out wants to expand that horizon without being educational. (Or ‘edifying’…) Peter Zumthor is an ideal guide to start thinking from scratch about what houses do to us, how they influence and form us. Zumthor’s discussion of creating inner security and safety for me immediately evokes for me the specter of its opposite, the unsafe spaces, the spaces of destruction, the homes flattened in Ukraine, Yemen, Lebanon and Gaza. How would you respond to the critique that Zumthor’s serene spaces of peace and contemplation are also an expression of extreme privilege, and a way of avoiding the ugliness and darkness in the world? The question of privilege is a legitimate one. Who has access to safety, to shelter, to places of peace and contemplation – and who doesn’t? When we look at the destruction of homes and living spaces caused by wars – in Ukraine, Yemen, Lebanon, Gaza and elsewhere – we are not only looking at the destruction of buildings. We are looking at the destruction of places: places where people lived, where families and communities came together, places of memory, of belonging and of everyday life. The loss of safety, home and community is devastating for civilians wherever it happens. And perhaps that is precisely why the question of what a human space can be is not less relevant in such a world, but even more urgent! What interests me in Zumthor’s architecture is not simply beauty or contemplation. His buildings ask what spaces can do for human beings – how they can offer shelter and protection, but also create a sense of belonging, encounter and community. Of course, as a European filmmaker I am speaking from a privileged position. And I would never pretend that art or architecture can undo the destruction of people’s homes or repair the suffering caused by war. But they can be a response to it – a gesture that opposes destruction and cynicism with another idea of how we might live together. Zumthor’s buildings, in my book, speak the language of believing in a better version of humanity. The best critique of existing “ugliness and darkness” can also be to present “beauty and light” as alternatives. That is my firm conviction as a filmmaker. Take Zumthor’s Kolumba Museum in Cologne. If you walk in with the blues, disenchanted, hopeless or even in despair, you might find yourself walking out restored. Yes, I believe a building can do that. Architecture can remind us of the version of humanity we are aspiring to. The new David Geffen Galleries at LACMA offer another example: a museum without the usual hierarchies, conceived in the congenial collaboration between its director, Michael Govan, and its architect, Peter Zumthor. Now, on one floor, you can cross the planet and its art without one culture being privileged over another. ONE PLACE for all – like our world should be. Buildings cannot repair the world. But they can change our idea of what the world could be. What do you hope an audience takes away from this film? I hope… that they gain hope. A lot of things on this planet can or should get better. Especially our respect for nature, for the other, and for our sense of kindness and decency. In a shitty world, a visit to a good place can do wonders. The film – I hope – can instigate an appreciation for architecture that lets us see the difference between ‘more of the same’ and ‘something that makes a difference’. All of us can make a difference. All of us can care. Here, an architect tries to do that. That is encouraging. THR

title: May el-Toukhy Takes ‘Woman Unknown’ to Venice: “I’ve Used Every Part of Me to Make This Film”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 6, 2026 1:00am May El-Toukhy Photographer: Søren Rønholt Danish filmmaker May el-Toukhy , one of the two female directors competing for the Golden Lion this year, in Venice with a sharp, searing analysis of the women thrown to the wolves in the aftermath of World War II. Women Unknown — Scandinavian in both its aesthetic and precision — was always going to be about class, complicity and survival. For a brief period, it was even going to focus on the Reformation witch hunts, before el-Toukhy found herself a little bored by the perpetrators. “The reasons they were hunting these women were just not that interesting,” she laughs to The Hollywood Reporter . Related Stories Movies Liam and Noel Gallagher Lock Arms at Venice Premiere of 'Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger' Movies 'Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger' Review: A Rich and Poignant Celebration of a Beloved Band's Glorious and Improbable Return Inspired by a newspaper picture dated from the 1940s of a woman sitting with a swastika painted on her back, el-Toukhy and co-writer Maren Louise Käehne soon turned their attention to the women whose bodies became a battlefield during the Second World War; those who found themselves with no choice but to fall into the arms of soldiers from occupying armies, and suffered severe consequences — hunted down, publicly shamed and punished for the rest of their lives. Woman Unknown is backdropped by a Danish city free from Nazi occupation, mere months after World War II has ended. It tells the story of Marie (Mathilde Arcel), a young nanny and housemaid about to marry her wealthy, older, and widowed employer, Christian (Carsten Bjørnlund). But Marie guards a shameful secret. During the war, she was in an intimate relationship with a German soldier. Now Marie’s past threatens to catch up with her, and she is forced to do everything in her power to preserve her new status as lady of the house in post-war anarchy. It is as much about resistance and patriotism in a euphoric, liberated Europe as it is about the chastisement of women and their sex lives. El-Toukhy is adamant that this is a story about the female experience. “There have been so many films about the Second World War, and that is true. But they’re all based mostly on men’s experiences and recollections of war. So that really energized me,” she says. “Let’s just do another 100 films about the women in this time period, and then we can say we’re over and done with it, you know?” A co-production between Denmark, Sweden and Latvia, financing the film wasn’t the tallest hurdle — but el-Toukhy has learned to be economical with her resources at a time when filmmaking costs have never higher. With her third feature film, following Long Story Short (2015) and Queen of Hearts (2019), she comes to the Lido buoyed by the hope that Woman Unknown will produce debate. El-Toukhy spoke to THR about the far-and-wide casting search for Marie, why she feels she’s already won before even stepping foot in Italy and whether those nerves have begun to kick in: “I’ve worked 16 hours a day for more than a year. I’ve spent all my savings. I’ve used every part of me to make this film and all the resources, all the muscle power I have. I can’t really do any more, so therefore I feel okay.” I’m curious about this period of Danish history, and whether you learned about it at school. Why use it as a backdrop for this film? After my last film, I thought I was going to do a film on the witch hunts after the Reformation, in the middle of [the] 1500s, and so I started researching that subject matter. But I found it quite hard to engage with the perpetrators because the reasons they were hunting these women were just not that interesting. ( Laughs .) At that time, me and my co-writer were slowly moving away from that idea, and then while we were moving away from that idea, some photos got republished in the newspaper with a woman who was sitting on a bench with a swastika painted on her back. And she [had been] assaulted in these photographs. Those [were] the propaganda photos that were produced in 1943. So we were reminded of that issue. It is something that we do learn in school here. It’s part of the curriculum — to deal with the First World War, Second World War, the events between the two wars and the aftermath, but often the aftermath here, in schools, would be focused on the politics, the collaboration the Danish government chose at that time and also the resistance movement. We didn’t spend too much time in school dealing with or talking about [or] debating the destiny of these women. I’m always interested in investigating something that takes a lot for me to engage in; that’s difficult material. Where there’s no black and white, but everything is gray. And you chose to depict that woman in that photograph in the film. Yeah. In the propaganda photos, they were reproducing this image of a woman who has been assaulted, but then when I started digging, [I found] an archive [of them]… I think what’s interesting about the situation itself is it’s a societal, structural mob mentality. It’s fellow citizens who are punishing these women. It doesn’t come from the government. The government actually tried to remove these women from the streets — to protect them — but they didn’t manage very well. And sometimes, even on the way to a camp, a woman would be assaulted, even though she was supposed to be protected by the government. For me, it was quite important to really show an audience what this feels like. They didn’t get killed, these women, but their souls were hurt and they were stigmatized and traumatized for life. How did you find your way to Marie as a character, and her story? I think there’s a class aspect in the story that I’m very drawn to, and also I had that thematic base in my last film. She’s a young woman who is moving away from the area she knows and her family and takes a job in a big city. [She] probably feels protected by living in a big city compared to being at home where she can be more exposed. She’s a woman who is struggling to survive. I might not agree with some of her actions, but I completely understand where that survival instinct comes from, and the idea that she wants to protect what she’s fought to obtain. Mathilde Arcel as Marie in ‘Woman Unknown’ Venice Film Festival What went into that casting search for Marie, and why was Mathilde right for it? As the title suggests, she’s very elusive for much of the film, up until her unraveling. I always have quite extensive casting processes, partly because I come from theater, but also because I really enjoy [it]. Casting a lead is, for me, like casting a creative partner. So I have to fall in love with the gaze of that person and their take on the character, and therefore I do many rounds and many callbacks. I did that with Mathilde as well, and some of it was improv, some of it was table readings, some of it was written scenes. I think what’s fantastic about Mathilde is that she has so much mystery to her and the way she’s chosen to interpret the character inspired me as a writer-director. That collaboration is key for me, and therefore I spend a lot of time figuring out which direction I want to go [in]. I’ve really enjoyed working with her, and I think she’s extremely talented. So mysterious but so expressive too. Yes, yes. One of the themes that stood out to me was complicity and what it means to be complicit when that head-down mentality is still so entrenched and the hangover of the war so menacing. What were you trying to speak to in this context? The film is not so much [about] giving answers to what’s right and wrong, but to debate what’s right and wrong, or what’s possibly right and what’s possibly wrong. It’s all a bit murky and muddy. Throughout the development of the film, it’s been quite important for me to to not tell the audience — or the readers, in the development of the script — what they should think, but create a situation where the audience can dive into that discussion with themselves or the people they’ve watched the film with. And it’s not only in that time, because I think it’s present also today — in many conflicts. It’s quite hard to to say that it’s just one thing, and the ability to contain two opposite thoughts at the same time is quite hard. Both can be true, and that’s my ambition with the film. Obviously, I have my own opinion about what’s going on in the film, but I think it’s quite important for me as a storyteller that there is room for reflection for the audience. It’s also very much a female-driven story. Do you think this is a period of history for women that isn’t depicted on screen enough? Is it an underrepresented story you’re telling? When I first started the process of developing the script with my co-writer, I would pitch the idea when people ask me: “What are you doing? What are you working on right now?” I started to semi-pitch it, just to see how people would react and what they respond to. And I could see that they would glaze over. ( Laughs .) They would have this empty gaze, because I think there have been so many films about the Second World War, and that is true. But they’re all based mostly on men’s experiences and recollections of war. So that really energized me. Yes, there have been a lot of films about this period [of history], but let’s just do another 100 films about the women in this time period, and then we can say we’re over and done with it, you know? The invisibility of women is everywhere, and certainly in cinema and in our films. So I don’t think we’re finished with the period, but it also sparked the idea of trying to make this film look different than a classical period piece, and to constantly disrupt the idea of a classical period piece. So that’s been an ongoing process of developing and shooting and in post[-production]. How long did it take you to get this film off the ground? I know it’s a co-production which must have helped. The process has been long, but not too long. I did my last film, then once it had premiered at Sundance and had the festival run and premiered in Denmark, I started to develop this film — first with the witch idea and then turning to these horizontal collaborators. Then COVID happened… I worked intensively on the script, and we [were in a place where we] could start the financing. But the financing part of it hasn’t been that difficult in the sense that we’ve had a lot of yeses. We’ve had so many people wanting to do this film. The problem in European cinema is that we don’t get very far with the money we get. There’s been an increase of costs after COVID, everything has gone up, and so we have to work faster in every part of the process. That’s been the challenge with this film, not so much getting the money, but getting far enough with the money we managed to get. What did it mean to you to find out this would be premiering in competition in Venice? I’m delighted that it’s part of this historic festival and that also this theme gets to be exposed for a European audience. I think it’s very important that we keep reminding ourselves of our past and these stories, so that we understand and we analyze and we debate to be able to handle the present and the future differently — if possible. I don’t think it is. But I’m really happy, [Venice is] the best place to be for European film right now. I’m excited. I have this place inside of me where I can go after I’ve made a film. I’ve spent all the time I possibly could on this film. I’ve worked 16 hours a day for more than a year. I’ve spent all my savings. I’ve used every part of me to make this film and all the resources, all the muscle power I have. I can’t really do any more, so therefore I feel okay. Slightly anxious, and I think that’s only natural. There must be a really liberating feeling of finally being able to send it out into the world. Yeah. And I think getting into the festival and being in competition, I’ve already won. How can exposure in Venice help a filmmaker like yourself and your career? [Festivals are] important for the arthouse [films] because it’s a market. It’s also a place where you, as a filmmaker, can create new relationships that you can build on later down the line. But for me, it’s really about the audience that’s there. Through a festival, you can access an audience if you have enough buyers that take the film and they then distribute it around the world. And I think it’s quite important for me as a filmmaker to cling on to [the audience], because it’s so easy to be distracted by other things that are equally nice and shiny and attractive. But especially the way we finance film in Scandinavia, where it’s publicly funded, I think it’s really important that these films find their audience. None of us have that crystal ball where we can look into it and say, “Okay, if I put this person into a film with this theme and shoot…” But that’s really the hope for me, that this film will find its audience. Are you already thinking about the next one? I can’t help thinking about the next and the next and the next, especially when I go cycling or walking or hiking. But I don’t have that much spare time right now. So, most of my energy is channelled into promoting this film. I’m in the service of this film still. The 2026 Venice Film Festival runs Sept. 2-12. THR

title: Are Russian Filmmakers Finally Coming in From the Cold?
full_text: Sep 6, 2026 12:45am PT Are Russian Filmmakers Finally Coming in From the Cold? Despite the controversy around a competition berth for Ilya Khrzhanovsky's "DAU" in Venice, top film festivals have increasingly welcomed back Russian filmmakers while the war in Ukraine drags on By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest Groundbreaking Roma Director Alina Șerban on ‘Pain,’ ‘Joy,’ of Historic, Venice-Bound ‘I Matter’: ‘I Managed to Do Something Impossible’ 6 hours ago Venice: ‘My Undesirable Friends’ Director on Epic Documentary About Death of Press Freedom in Russia, How Putin’s Crackdown Is Warning for U.S. 1 day ago AR Content, Vertigo, Blumhouse Atomic Monster Set Remake of Genre-Bending, Satirical French Horror ‘Vincent Must Die’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All Venice Film Festival The Venice Film Festival found itself under fire in the weeks leading up to opening night over the inclusion of “DAU,” by Russian filmmaker Ilya Khrzhanovsky , in the main competition of its 83rd edition. In a joint statement released on Aug. 17, the Ukraine Ministries of Foreign Affairs and Culture and the Ukrainian Embassy in Italy criticized the prestigious fest for selecting what they claimed to be “a project linked to the Russian state and its networks of influence,” maintaining that the decision helped to “restore respectability” to Putin’s pariah state. Popular on Variety Related Stories Dave Bautista Officially Set as Kratos in 'God of War' TV Series Dave Bautista Shows Off Body Transformation to Play Kratos in 'God of War' Series: 'Two More Months to Get to Where I Need to Be' The pushback was swift. In an Instagram post responding to the criticism, Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera insisted that “‘DAU’ is not a Russian film; it is not pro-Putin propaganda.” Meanwhile, Khrzhanovsky took to Facebook to refute allegations that the latest installment in his long-running project was backed by Russian financing or is “an instrument of Russian state cultural policy.” Speaking to Variety on the eve of the festival, the director — who renounced his Russian citizenship in 2024 — doubled down, saying: “Since the war started, there was no question of what side I am on, because I am on the side of Ukraine.” Coming on the heels of a recent controversy surrounding the Venice Art Biennale’s decision to mount shows by Russian and Israeli artists, the “DAU” dust-up speaks to a larger question hanging over film festivals, cultural institutions and other events that, in the immediate aftermath of Russia ’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, largely heeded calls for a boycott of Russian cultural exports. As the war drags deeper into its fifth year, a rapprochement of sorts is underway. While relations with Moscow remain frosty for much of the world, Russian filmmakers are gradually coming in from the cold. In the past year alone, Russian-born directors have scooped prizes in Venice (Nastia Korkia’s “Short Summer”) and Cannes ( Andrey Zvyagintsev ’s “Minotaur”), while Khrzhanovsky is joined on the Lido by fellow exile Victor Kossakovsky, whose latest documentary, “Holly Wood Dust,” premieres out of competition. Though the Oscar-nominated Kossakovsky (“Gunda”) and Khrzhanovsky both left Russia in the 2000s, a broader exodus began not long after Russian tanks rolled into Ukraine in February 2022. Whether fleeing in protest of the Kremlin’s war machine or out of fear of the brutal crackdown on dissent that quickly followed, many of Russian cinema’s most prominent voices left the country, forging exile communities from Tbilisi to Paris, from Berlin to L.A. “There are two Russias right now,” says two-time Oscar nominee Alexander Rodnyansky (“Leviathan”), in Venice with Kornél Mundruczó’s “Place to Be,” starring Ellen Burstyn and Taika Waititi. “Russia as the country with this regime controlling everything and censoring all the attempts to speak freely about what’s going on. And there is a Russia outside of the geographical borders.” That diaspora is experiencing exile in a variety of ways. The Kyiv-born Rodnyansky, who was sentenced in absentia to 8.5 years in prison by a Moscow court over his opposition to the war, remains determined to support dissenting voices and “make movies with Russian filmmakers, especially young ones, who I feel myself committed to help.” Now based in France, Zvyagintsev likewise remains a trenchant critic of a country he says he has “no intention” of returning to. Though filmed in Latvia, his Cannes Grand Prix-winning “ Minotaur ” is as scathing a portrait of Russian society under Putin as the director’s previous works. For other filmmakers, the westward flight has offered an opportunity for reinvention. Kantemir Balagov’s “ Butterfly Jam ,” which opened the Directors’ Fortnight section this year in Cannes, stars Barry Keoghan and Riley Keough and is set in an immigrant community in Newark. Director Kirill Sokolov likewise set off for Hollywood; his latest, the blood-soaked revenge farce “ They Will Kill You ,” stars Zazie Beetz and Patricia Arquette. Sokolov’s dark comedy “No Looking Back” was among the first films to bear the brunt of the anti-Russia backlash in 2022, when it was pulled from the Glasgow Film Festival over financing that came in part from the Putin regime. The “DAU” controversy in Venice was similarly driven by ties to Russian financiers who would later be sanctioned following the Ukraine invasion. But Khrzhanovsky stresses to Variety that their involvement in his decades-spanning project ended years ago; his Venice-bound film is a German production, co-produced with France and Sweden, and has received no Russian funding for seven years, according to the director. As these and other Russian filmmakers set up new lives in exile, the financial ties that once bound them to Putin’s state have been cut. That, as much as their vocal opposition to the Ukraine war, arguably weakens the case for protest and will ease further reentry into the international film community. “They’re shot in Europe. They’re financed in Europe,” says Laurent Danielou, of Paris-based Loco Films, who’s currently financing two features from émigré Russian directors. “They’re not Russian anymore.” ‘The Odyssey’ Anoints Christopher Nolan as Hollywood’s Most Powerful Director — Here’s How Universal Thwarted Warner Bros. to Land Him Matthew McConaughey’s First Screen Role Helped Catch a Murderer Christopher Nolan and ‘The Odyssey’ Cast Break Down Ties to ‘Oppenheimer,’ Elevating Homer’s Female Characters and Why Nolan Avoided Yelling ‘Cut!’ on Set ‘The Odyssey’ Translator Emily Wilson Slams Christoper Nolan’s ‘Abysmal’ Screenplay: ‘I Would Be Ashamed to Have Written Any Part of This Script’ ‘The Odyssey’ Screenplay Is Now Available to Buy Online Christopher Nolan Fans Will Stop at Nothing to See ‘The Odyssey’ in Imax 70mm, From Cross-Country Trips to Delaying Pregnancy Loading comments...
