title: ‘The Debut’ Review: Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti Are Dynamite Together in Jesse Eisenberg’s Entertainingly Offbeat Theater Comedy
full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All September 6, 2026 12:25am The Debut A24 When Mona ( Julianne Moore ) tells a friend she’s auditioned for a production of a show called Nosy Neighbors at their local theater, he admits he’s never liked musicals. They just don’t feel authentic, he explains, the way the characters are always bursting into song. Who does that? Well, no one, not even in the musical-loving The Debut . But among the first of the film’s sly tricks is that it builds a world in which it feels like people could , where in fact it feels more unnatural that they don’t. Blessed with swing-for-the-fences brio and, in Moore and Paul Giamatti , a leading duo capable of navigating every one of those wild turns, the latest feature by Jesse Eisenberg makes for a frequently hilarious journey into the mind of an overly committed actor — even if, in the end, it seems unsure quite what it wants to say about the self-destructive pursuit of artistic perfection. Related Stories Movies 'The Debut' Features Seven Original Songs, All Written by Jesse Eisenberg, and One Is Getting an Oscar Push (Exclusive) Movies 'The Row' Review: 'Icarus' Director Bryan Fogel's Doc Takes Viewers on a Gripping, Question-Raising Solo Voyage Across the Pacific The Debut The Bottom Line A very good time, if not necessarily a profound one. Venue: Telluride Film Festival Cast: Julianne Moore, Paul Giamatti, Halle Bailey, Jesse Eisenberg, Cara Buono, Craig Bierko, Eldar Isgandarov, Bernadette Peters Director-screenwriter: Jesse Eisenberg Rated R, 1 hour 45 minutes At first, Mona would seem an unlikely candidate to go Method in the way of certain prestige actors or comic book movie stars . When we meet her, she’s a meek suburban housewife who’s never acted a day in her life, and whose audition is so mediocre she doesn’t even realize how mediocre it is. Once she lands a relatively minor role anyway, owing to a twist of fate that she may have ever-so-slightly nudged along, she’s just happy to be there, drinking in any suggestion or note or friendly gesture extended to her. But even from the start, before Mona properly goes off the deep end, The Debut starts inuring us to her heightened perspective. When Mona gets the call saying she’s gotten the part, a spotlight floods her grin and the camera rushes in, as if she might start belting on the spot. On her first day of rehearsal, the whole world is lit a little brighter than it was a few scenes earlier. When she endears herself to her new colleagues with a joke, the laughter feels slightly too enthusiastic. The effect is almost eerie to start, and it takes some getting used to. But it turns out to be just the tip of the iceberg. The pivot comes when the production’s director, Jerry (Giamatti) — described in a low-key perfect bit of dialogue as “basically the biggest name in New Jersey community theater” — pulls Mona aside for the private special instruction that she (as a truly godawful singer and actress) so desperately needs. Jerry’s usual method is to break his actors down so he can “put Humpty Dumpty together again,” and it begins exactly as planned in an acting exercise that yields one of the very biggest laughs in a film rich with them. But then Mona takes a little too well to his guidance. As Mona loses herself in her character, a building superintendent named Miss Danielle, her wardrobe, courtesy of costume designer Stacey Battat, goes from prim cardigans to ripped jeans to an actual coverall she’s stolen from a janitor. (This is neither the first nor last time you’ll think to yourself, “Man, theater people are a menace ” and “Jesse Eisenberg’s seen some shit, huh?”) She begins frequenting a seedy motel that production designer Anne Ross has cleverly made into a theater actor’s exaggeratedly noirish version of what a seedy motel would look like, with smoke-blurred neon lights and a trash can fire outside and an inexplicably naked man roaming the halls inside. Most worryingly for Nosy Neighbors — in-universe a well-known musical that’s been around a few decades, in reality an original concocted by Eisenberg and seen here in perfectly cheesy snippets — Mona starts to question Miss Danielle’s motivations, then her lines, then her actions. Jerry realizes he’s created his own worst nightmare: the sort of difficult actor who thinks she knows her character better than the director or even the script that invented her. Lively throughout, The Debut ascends to new heights whenever Giamatti and Moore share the screen together. Moore is an absolute hoot as Mona, who starts out looking on paper like one of those disaffected housewives she’s played so often (and so expertly) in her career but turns out to be much, much stranger. Giamatti makes Jerry ferocious but not monstruous, a man who certainly likes barking orders at various underlings but loves making good theater even more. Their scenes opposite each other are not just entertaining but thrillingly dynamic, as the balance of power between them begins to shift. It’s all so much fun that it’s easy not to notice at first that none of this is headed anywhere particularly profound. There’s a touch of poignancy in the understanding that Mona is so eager to lose herself in Miss Danielle because — like Rita , the protagonist of Telluride 2026’s other “New Jersey suburbanite abandons her family to pursue a more authentic life under the guidance of a charismatic but demanding leader” premiere — she barely knows who she is in the first place. But the film never builds out the rest of Mona’s world, like her inattentive husband (Patrick Fabian), or even co-stars like Steph (a very endearing Halle Bailey) and Todd (Eisenberg, adorably giving himself an excuse to sing and dance), to take that line of thinking anywhere truly insightful or emotional. Among the arguments between Mona and Jerry are what theater can or should be. Mona argues that that the stories it tell should be “real,” even at the expense of a happy ending, while Jerry argues that no one cares much about the plot — audiences just want to feel while spying on the intimate lives of other people. The Debut , in prioritizing style, humor and outrageous plot turns over complex emotionality, would seem to side with Jerry. Maybe it’s not everything it could be. But as I howled over the lengths Mona would go to for the sake of what Jerry unkindly but accurately points out is, in the end, just some “thankless tertiary character,” it felt like more than enough. Full credits Venue: Telluride Film Festival Distributor: A24 Production companies: Fruit Tree, Topic Studios Cast: Julianne Moore, Paul Giamatti, Halle Bailey, Jesse Eisenberg, Cara Buono, Craig Bierko, Eldar Isgandarov, Bernadette Peters Director-screenwriter: Jesse Eisenberg Producers: Emma Stone, Dave McCary, Ali Herting, Jesse Eisenberg Executive producers: Michael Bloom, Ian Stratford, Ryan Heller, Jasmine Daghighian, Jennifer Booth, Kevin Kelly Director of photography: Drew Daniels Production designer: Anne Ross Costume designer: Stacey Battat Editor: Robert Nassau Music: Emile Mosseri Casting director: Douglas Aibel Sound mixer: Dimitri Kouri Rated R, 1 hour 45 minutes THR

title: Groundbreaking Roma Director Alina Șerban on ‘Pain,’ ‘Joy,’ of Historic, Venice-Bound ‘I Matter’: ‘I Managed to Do Something Impossible’
full_text: Sep 5, 2026 11:35pm PT Groundbreaking Roma Director Alina Șerban on ‘Pain,’ ‘Joy,’ of Historic, Venice-Bound ‘I Matter’: ‘I Managed to Do Something Impossible’ By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest Groundbreaking Roma Director Alina Șerban on ‘Pain,’ ‘Joy,’ of Historic, Venice-Bound ‘I Matter’: ‘I Managed to Do Something Impossible’ 6 hours ago Venice: ‘My Undesirable Friends’ Director on Epic Documentary About Death of Press Freedom in Russia, How Putin’s Crackdown Is Warning for U.S. 1 day ago AR Content, Vertigo, Blumhouse Atomic Monster Set Remake of Genre-Bending, Satirical French Horror ‘Vincent Must Die’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All Courtesy Young Nomads Roma filmmaker Alina Șerban broke barriers long before she set foot on the red carpet this week at the Venice Film Festival , where her feature-length directorial debut, “I Matter,” world premieres in the Venice Spotlight section. Rising from an impoverished background to become a celebrated stage star in Romania, the actress and directing debutante has defied all odds to reach the starry heights of the Lido. Billed as the first feature from a female Roma director to screen at an A-list festival, “I Matter” marks the latest chapter in her life-long quest to reframe the narrative around her marginalized community. Related Stories Dave Bautista Officially Set as Kratos in 'God of War' TV Series Dave Bautista Shows Off Body Transformation to Play Kratos in 'God of War' Series: 'Two More Months to Get to Where I Need to Be' Șerban, however, is taking it all in stride. Popular on Variety “I’m nervous about the pressure of being ‘the first’ — all the firsts,” she tells Variety . “But I also have this immense relief, and the feeling of being grateful that I managed to pull through something almost impossible.” Inspired by Șerban’s own life, “I Matter” tells the story of a young Roma woman studying to be an actor. She’s faced with the threat of being kicked out of her orphanage and must suddenly embrace her identity and confront the reality of making it through life on her own. Based on the 2021 short of the same name, whose festival run included New Directors/New Films, it’s produced by microFILM, 2Pilots Filmproduction, Frakas Prods. and Lemming Film, with international sales handled by Pluto Film. For Șerban, the premiere is a capstone in what has already been a remarkable career. Raised in poverty in Bucharest, she was placed in a state-run orphanage at an early age before becoming the first member of her family to graduate from high school. After attending Bucharest’s Academy of Theatrical Arts and Cinematography, she was accepted into NYU’s Tisch School of the Arts, then later earned a master’s degree from the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London. When she returned to Romania, she mounted an acclaimed one-woman show about her life, focusing not only on the rampant discrimination she faced, but on her triumphs and joys. By her 30th birthday, Șerban had written and staged pioneering plays that championed a radical, feminist, Roma perspective — trying, she says, “to show the humanity of these people. Not to portray them as victims nor villains. Not to self-exoticize. But also to celebrate ourselves.” “I Matter” stars newcomer Denisa Farcaș, bringing both vulnerability and determination to a lead role that she invests with her own life experience, according to the director. Șerban describes working with Farcaș and her co-stars as a “collaborative process,” one in which the group delved deep into “what it means to be accepted” as Roma women while giving the young actors space to “express themselves — to feel that they also own the story.” This isn’t Șerban’s first visit to the Venice Film Festival; she attended in 2023 with the cast and crew of Goran Stolevski’s “Housekeeping for Beginners,” in which she had a supporting role. But this year’s experience will be something else entirely for the director. Nearly two dozen of the cast members of “I Matter” will be in attendance — including the 16 child performers who populated the film’s orphanage — while Roma band Mahala Rai Banda will serenade the red-carpet arrivals. “This is such a historical moment for me, and also for the Roma community,” Șerban says. “It’s a moment of celebration. And I want to look back and say I did everything in my power for the people in the team to [share this] moment. title: Moonfish’ Director and Stars Lucy Liu and Morgan Spector Break Down Their Black-and-White Animated Film About Isolated Astronauts And Why It’s an Allegory for ‘The Current Human Condition’
full_text: Sep 5, 2026 11:05pm PT Moonfish’ Director and Stars Lucy Liu and Morgan Spector Break Down Their Black-and-White Animated Film About Isolated Astronauts And Why It’s an Allegory for ‘The Current Human Condition’ By Matt Minton Plus Icon Matt Minton mminton@variety.com Latest Moonfish’ Director and Stars Lucy Liu and Morgan Spector Break Down Their Black-and-White Animated Film About Isolated Astronauts And Why It’s an Allegory for ‘The Current Human Condition’ 7 hours ago The Rise of ‘Love Island USA’: From Death Threats Against Contestants to Agency Battles for the Biggest Stars 6 days ago ‘Lanterns’ Stars Aaron Pierre, Jasmine Cephas Jones on John’s Backstory Episode and How Being Black Informs His Quest to Become Green Lantern: ‘Fear Is Instilled in Our Ancestry’ 6 days ago See All Venice Film Festival For Lucy Liu, who has voiced memorable characters in everything from “Kung Fu Panda” to “Strange World,” being part of the independently made, black-and-white animated film “ Moonfish ” was all about lending her name and support to first-time filmmaker Daniel Zvereff. “These are the people that are not just the creatives, but the ones who are going to be the future,” Liu tells Variety . “I’m just fascinated by how people work and how things start when there’s not all this red tape.” Related Stories ‘The Truffle Hunters’ Directors Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw Look for the Perfect Wine in ‘Burgundy’: ‘A Great Glass of Wine Changes How You Perceive the World’ Venice Market Chief Pascal Diot Says He's Not Affected by New Toronto Market: 'Not What the Industry Wants Now' Premiering at the Venice Film Festival on Sept. 6 after receiving a grant from Biennale College Cinema, “Moonfish” follows a pair of astronauts, voiced by Liu and “The Gilded Age” star Morgan Spector, as they embark on an isolating mission to the moon with a corporate quota to meet if they want to return home. Popular on Variety “I really wanted to have the film take place in an environment that was an allegory to our current human condition we’re all experiencing right now, where society is very plugged in, but simultaneously we’re all growing a bit disconnected,” Zvereff says. Zvereff designed the 2D-animated film so that he could finish it completely on his own, if need be. Thankfully, as Zvereff worked over the course of nine months, he managed to bring on two animators, Hoss Wheeler and Devin Grover. “When I watch 2D-animated films, I feel like I’m being exposed to the subconscious of that artist,” Zvereff says of his approach. Liu adds, “It’s amazing what digital has done for the speed of animation but you can really feel the appreciation and the craftsmanship [here]. There is a tenderness and an imperfection that I appreciate.” Unlike Liu, Spector had never done an animated film before “Moonfish.” The trickiest part was getting into his character’s mental headspace as he goes “a little mad,” as Spector puts it. “This particular class of people has come to live on the moon, and they’ve evolved, essentially, as moon people. But they’ve also evolved as an underclass; they are the group of people without rights, assets or any real hope for the future,” Spector says of Zvereff’s worldbuilding. Liu, of course, also voices the talking fish that accompanies the pair (which Zvereff likens to how miners brought along canaries to know when they had to leave) amidst the mundanity of the corporate tasks at hand. “The future that Daniel’s imagining is one in which the relationship between human beings and their tools has been totally inverted. The corporation has merged with the computer in a sort of perfect authoritarian machine that uses human beings as fodder, basically,” Spector says. “It’s a vision of the world that feels continuous with the one we live in.” While the film explores isolation and loneliness in space, with the dialogue sparse and to-the-point, Zvereff realized during the writing process that it needed to ultimately be positive about the future of humanity. “That’s something that happens as an artist. title: Dev Benegal’s Judith Blum Reddy Doc ‘Everything Is Not OK’ Acquired by Watermelon Pictures, Annemarie Jacir Aboard as EP (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 5, 2026 10:50pm PT Dev Benegal’s Judith Blum Reddy Doc ‘Everything Is Not OK’ Acquired by Watermelon Pictures, Annemarie Jacir Aboard as EP (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Dev Benegal’s Judith Blum Reddy Doc ‘Everything Is Not OK’ Acquired by Watermelon Pictures, Annemarie Jacir Aboard as EP (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago San Sebastian, Busan-Bound Taiwanese Coming-of-Age Drama ‘Will You Still Be My Friend’ Boarded for Sales by Moveria, Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago Lee Chang-dong, Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu on Class, Desire and Reunion in Venice Competition Drama ‘Possible Love’ 7 hours ago See All Min(d) Studio Watermelon Pictures has acquired “ Everything Is Not OK ,” a documentary from director Dev Benegal chronicling the life of artist Judith Blum Reddy . The film will stream exclusively on Watermelon+, the distributor’s streaming platform. The producing team pairs Benegal with Min(d) Studio’s Maya S. Patel and Neeraj Jain, while Annemarie Jacir (“Palestine 36”) has signed on as executive producer. Related Stories Dave Bautista Officially Set as Kratos in 'God of War' TV Series Dave Bautista Shows Off Body Transformation to Play Kratos in 'God of War' Series: 'Two More Months to Get to Where I Need to Be' “Everything Is Not OK” follows Reddy, whose work as an artist has been shaped by the Holocaust and by displacements that carried her from New York to Paris and ultimately India. The documentary threads Reddy’s story together with those of fellow artists Nil Yalter, Zarina and Camille Billops, each of whom channeled displacement into their art. Palestinian, Kashmiri and Indian poets are interwoven throughout, framing the film as a meditation on remembering what has been erased from home and pushing back once staying quiet stops being an option. Popular on Variety “For Judy, making art is an act of confrontation. An act of liberation. A refusal to let erasure win,” Benegal said. “‘Everything Is Not OK’ is not only a portrait of an artist — it is a meditation on what it means to create, remember and resist through art when silence is no longer an option.” Jacir signed on as executive producer after connecting with the film’s exploration of memory and resistance. “In a moment when the world tilts towards intolerance, Judy’s story is a reminder that memory refuses to disappear and art can still be an act of resistance,” Jacir said. Jacir and actor Adam Bakri both lend their voices to the film’s readings of revolutionary poetry. Benegal is also known for directing “English, August” and “Road, Movie.” A restored version of “English, August,” undertaken by the Film Heritage Foundation, is playing at the Venice Film Festival . The 1994 film is based on Upamanyu Chatterjee’s novel “English, August: An Indian Story” and stars Rahul Bose. The creative team behind “Everything Is Not OK” includes Jain doubling as producer and additional cinematography; Patel as producer; Dhruv Goel composing the music; Jean-Luc Panda as cinematographer; Mona Gesbel as editor; Anurag Jadhao on sound design; and Rob Sciarratta as colorist. Watermelon Pictures launched in 2024. Its distribution and production credits include “From Ground Zero” and “All That’s Left of You” alongside “Palestine 36,” all three shortlisted in the Academy Award’s international feature category, plus the Oscar-nominated “The Voice of Hind Rajab.” Hamza Ali and co-founder Badie Ali brought the Watermelon+ platform online in May 2025, positioning it as the largest single collection of Palestinian film ever assembled in one place. title: San Sebastian, Busan-Bound Taiwanese Coming-of-Age Drama ‘Will You Still Be My Friend’ Boarded for Sales by Moveria, Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 5, 2026 10:48pm PT San Sebastian, Busan-Bound Taiwanese Coming-of-Age Drama ‘Will You Still Be My Friend’ Boarded for Sales by Moveria, Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Dev Benegal’s Judith Blum Reddy Doc ‘Everything Is Not OK’ Acquired by Watermelon Pictures, Annemarie Jacir Aboard as EP (EXCLUSIVE) 7 hours ago San Sebastian, Busan-Bound Taiwanese Coming-of-Age Drama ‘Will You Still Be My Friend’ Boarded for Sales by Moveria, Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE) 7 hours ago Lee Chang-dong, Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu on Class, Desire and Reunion in Venice Competition Drama ‘Possible Love’ 7 hours ago See All Moveria Paris-based Moveria has boarded international sales on Taiwanese filmmaker Lu Po-Shun’s debut feature “ Will You Still Be My Friend ,” which is set for a berth in San Sebastián’s New Directors sidebar before travelling on to the Busan International Film Festival . A Taiwan-Singapore co-production, the film follows two young boys, played by Jaden Wang and Aloysius Looi, whose bond comes under strain as tensions build between their families and the surrounding rural community. Rounding out the cast are Lung Tien Hsiang, Lu Yi-Ching, Andie Chen, Kate Pang and Xing Chang. Related Stories Chloé Zhao Defends Comic-Book Movies: 'It's Important to Not Write Off Stories Because We Don't Consider Them High Art' Lee Chang-dong, Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu on Class, Desire and Reunion in Venice Competition Drama 'Possible Love' A trailer has been unveiled. Popular on Variety Eric Chou Tseng-Chen and Yu-Hao Su produced the film through Taiwan-based InLight Film Studio and Verdant Peak Films. At San Sebastián, the film is also in contention for the Sebastiane Award, an honor for films exploring LGBTQIA+ themes and experiences. In the story, an escalating feud in a rural Taiwanese village forces a boy to shield his secret friendship with his Singapore-raised best friend from the adult conflicts threatening to divide them, even as he privately begins to question his own feelings for his friend. “What I really connected with is the relationship between the two boys,” said Yasmin Porangaba, Moveria’s head of sales and acquisition. “When they’re alone, everything feels simple, light and natural. It’s like they have this little world of their own, almost like a secret, because the people around them don’t really get them. Around their families and friends, they have to fit into certain roles, while their time together feels like a space where none of that matters. “I also love that the film never defines what they are to each other. They’re too young to really make sense of it themselves, and I like that the film leaves that open. They know how to be there for each other, forgive each other and just move forward in a way that feels surprisingly mature. The two boys are amazing together, the film is beautiful, and that’s really what made us want to represent it.” The film has already built an international industry profile through selections including Ties That Bind, the Golden Horse Film Project Promotion, EFM Far East in Progress and HAF Goes to Cannes at the Cannes Film Market. Lu’s short film “Wild Tides” earlier earned him the best director prize at the Taipei Film Awards. He also directed the segment “Way Home” in the 2018 anthology film “Ten Years Taiwan,” part of Busan’s A Window on Asian Cinema lineup. “Will You Still Be My Friend” is his first feature as director. Producer Eric Chou Tseng-Chen brings experience in sales, acquisitions, project management and festival promotion on the international circuit, and co-produced “Get the Hell Out,” which had its bow in the Midnight Madness lineup at Toronto in 2020. Yu-Hao Su has produced credits such as Shatara Michelle Ford’s “Test Pattern,” a Film Independent Spirit Award and Gotham Award nominee, as well as “Fragrance of the First Flower.” Su also executive produced Ford’s “Dreams in Nightmares,” which screened in Berlinale’s Panorama section. InLight Film Studio, a Taiwan-based outfit, spans film and visual art projects, while Verdant Peak Films is dedicated to bringing Taiwanese stories to global audiences and developing international co-productions. Verdant Peak’s recent credits include “Dreams in Nightmares.” Moveria, headquartered in Paris, operates as an independent production and sales outfit for international markets. The synoptic gospels are Matthew, Mark, and Luke.” Related Stories News Mel Gibson Apologizes For "Thoughtless Idiocy" After Seemingly Mocking ASL Interpreter At Fan Event News Mel Gibson Shares 'Lethal Weapon 5' Update: "I Think That The Fifth Script Is Better Than All Of The Others" Gibson seems to be saying that his upcoming two part film event, The Resurrection of the Christ , will seek to fill in some of the narrative between the various tellings. title: ‘A Tale of Two Cities’ Review: Kit Harington Has Done Far, Far Better Things Than This Bland MGM+ Dickens Adaptation
full_text: × Skip to main content By Daniel Fienberg Plus Icon Daniel Fienberg Chief Television Critic TheFienPrint Follow Sign Up View All September 5, 2026 8:43pm François Civil and Kit Harington of 'A Tale of Two Cities.' MGM+ Logo text MGM+ and BBC One’s A Tale of Two Cities is neither the best of adaptations nor the worst of adaptations, but Daniel West’s take on the Charles Dickens classic may well be the meh-est of adaptations. The four-part series benefits somewhat from the lack of an instantly identifiable definitive filmed interpretation of A Tale of Two Cities (depending on how you feel, I suppose, about the best picture-nominated 1935 feature) — a minor oddity given that the novel is in many ways Dickens’ most streamlined, featuring one of his best beginnings, best endings and most approachable narrative hooks. Related Stories TV Kit Harington Cast in 'Harry Potter' Season 2 as Gilderoy Lockhart, Replacing Nicholas Hoult TV Kit Harington Gets Caught in Love Triangle in 'Tale of Two Cities' Trailer A Tale of Two Cities The Bottom Line Fails to stand out as a romance, thriller or period piece. Airdate: Sunday, September 6 (MGM+) Cast: Francois Civil, Kit Harington, Mirren Mack, Roxane Duran Creator: Daniel West It’s a love triangle and a thriller set against the backdrop of the French Revolution. It features the usual Dickensian melange of colorful characters, breathless cliffhangers, shocking twists (not Oliver) and trenchant social commentary. It’s very much the epitome of a ripping yarn. Ultimately, though, freedom from negative comparisons to previous adaptations is not enough to prevent this take on A Tale of Two Cities from being a bland disappointment — one of the least Dickensian adaptations of a Charles Dickens work since Steven Knight adapted A Christmas Carol around the question, “What if Ebenezer Scrooge could say ‘fuck’?” It’s still a love story, but with virtually no passion between any of its three principals; and while it may be a tale of two cities, they both look like nearly identically designed stages in a warehouse in some affordable Eastern European country. For those who haven’t read A Tale of Two Cities or seen one of the forgettable previous adaptations — none, apparently, since a 1989 take that aired in the States under the Masterpiece Theatre banner — the plot is at once simple and convoluted. After a brief prelude in Paris in 1764, in which a young Lucie Manette watches her father apparently be killed, the action jumps forward 18 years. Lucie ( Mirren Mack ) is now living in London hoping to follow in her late father’s footsteps as a doctor. Lucie’s concrete interest in medicine is not, if memory serves, a part of a book in which she’s a more nebulous “healer,” nor is it all that relevant to the series after a strange introduction in which she’s practicing surgery on a corpse. It’s a nearly pointless choice, one of many. Lucie is living with Mrs. Lorry (Sharon Duncan-Brewster) and doing just fine for herself when her life is turned upside down with the arrival of Charles Darnay (François Civil). Charles is working on behalf of French revolutionaries, embodied by Roxane Duran’s Madame Defarge, to smuggle a generally irrelevant woman to safety in England. He’s also bearing a letter that suggests that Lucie’s dad (Yannick Renier) isn’t actually dead. The letter contains the evocative words “recalled to life,” which are potent on the page and nearly meaningless in the series. At the English border, Charles is wounded, which lets Lucie utilize her medical knowledge briefly. Then he’s arrested as a spy. Lucie seeks out legal representation for the heroic Charles, but finds only the generally drunk and uncouth Sydney Carton ( Kit Harington ). Both Charles and Sydney immediately fall in love with Lucie, because she’s somewhat the protagonist of the story and she’s pretty. Lucie, for her part, falls in love with both Charles and Sydney, which makes a little bit of sense since they look almost identical (assuming they aren’t standing next to each other, allowing one to see that Civil is a lot taller) and they’re both in constant need of chaste undressing. It makes less sense, though, because nothing in her interactions with either man comes across as the least bit romantic and the chemistry between Mack, Civil and Harington is wholly lacking, regardless of the permutation. As Lucie is reunited with her father, seriously psychologically damaged by his two decades in the Bastille, she learns shocking truths about Charles and his lineage and about the revolutionary motivations of Madame Defarge, whose general intransigence has caused her to be viewed as the villain of the piece, regardless of logic. Watching A Tale of Two Cities , it’s almost impossible to gauge what attracted West and the producers to the book, other than the IP and the reality that there are only so many times one can adapt Great Expectations , David Copperfield , Oliver Twist and A Christmas Carol before it becomes necessary to cycle back into the Dickens catalogue. The inspiration is nowhere to be found here. And A Tale of Two Cities is, as I’ve already said, a ripping yarn, featuring doppelgängers and surprises and the French blooming Revolution — featured in one thoroughly lifeless scene — plus it’s eternally timely since the story is one of those reliable Dickens screeds in which the impoverished masses are on the verge of toppling the heartless elite. Madame Defarge is — whether or not you buy her as a villain — one of fiction’s great adversaries, and her backstory is, itself, both eternally timely and specifically timely at a historical moment when you might have noticed one or two headlines about immoral wealthy men preying on defenseless young women. One could certainly adapt A Tale of Two Cities in a way that steers into the complications of Madame Defarge as a character, resulting in something that might almost resemble Hulu’s summer hit, Furious . She is, as a character, at best a righteous crusader and at worst a rigid zealot, but she’s hard to make uninteresting. Duran captures Defarge’s rage and, in a series plagued by thinly sketched characterizations hers comes closest to rising to the level of interesting. But her cause and her connection to that cause are mechanical pieces of the plot here, making it impossible to hate her or empathize with her. She’s just the person stirring up trouble whenever we go to Paris. Plus, it’s hard to know when we’re in Paris. As directed by Richard Clark, A Tale of Two Cities is temporally choppy and fails to build any emotional or geographical momentum. Though two cities are in the title, we’re treated to maybe a block or two of London and a block or two of Paris, visually interchangeable in a way that offers no real tangible connection to either staged location. Presumably, making Paris and London interchangeable is intentional, a parallel to the similarities between Charles and Sydney? Except that the entire purpose of the story’s arc is that one should be able to chart the life Charles was born into and the changes he made (all before the start of the story, since he’s pretty much stagnant onscreen throughout) and compare that to Sydney’s journey from the man he is when we meet him to the man he becomes by the end of the tale. In this case, though, since Harington and Civil are comparably solemn and earnest throughout — the actors do, if nothing else, look as similar as the story necessitates — there isn’t much evolution to trace. There are supposed to be comparable parallels to the arcs of Lucie and Madame Defarge, one as a force of optimistic good and the other as a force of all-consuming vengeance, but neither progression is all that engaging. Like Duran, Mack brings a little fire to the series, but Lucie is one of those Dickensian women who are unexplained rays of light who exist mostly to fuel the growth of the main male characters. As for the supporting ensemble from the page, from the bloodthirsty revolutionaries collectively known as Jacques to Sydney’s partner Mr. Stryver (a wasted Fehinti Balogun) to the figure known as The Vengeance, they’re either gone entirely or written so thinly here as to leave no impression. A Tale of Two Cities is in such a hurry to get from that memorable opening (rendered poorly as a voiceover at the end of the first episode) to that tremendous closing (rendered poorly as another voiceover) that the adaptation might as well have been as a two-hour movie. Certainly the cliffhangers at the end of each episode lack the urgency that Dickens himself understood so well how to evoke. The story itself is probably good enough to pull some viewers along from episode to episode, but the telling definitely is not good enough to inspire anybody to seek out MGM+. Regardless, there’s a far, far better adaptation of A Tale of Two Cities than has ever been done. This is not it. THR

full_text: × Skip to main content By Kirsten Chuba Plus Icon Kirsten Chuba Events Editor kirstenchuba Follow Sign Up View All September 5, 2026 8:00pm Mariska Hargitay, winner of the Outstanding Documentary Or Nonfiction Special award for "My Mom Jayne: A Film By Mariska Hargitay", poses in the Winner's Walk during the 78th Emmy Awards Night 1 at Peacock Theater on September 05, 2026 in Los Angeles, California Amy Sussman/Getty Images Mariska Hargitay is going into her Emmys hosting gig as a winner. The star, who is helming the Primetime Emmys on Sept. 14, took home two prizes at the Creative Arts Emmys for My Mom Jayne : A Film By Mariska Hargitay . She landed wins for directing for a documentary/nonfiction program and for outstanding documentary or nonfiction special; the night brings Hargitay’s career Emmy total to three, after she won best actress for Law & Order: Special Victims Unit in 2006. “It feels extraordinarily new and it’s deeply meaningful for me to have gone into a completely different arena, and to be recognized like this is really beyond my wildest dreams,” she told reporters backstage of how these two trophies compare to her one from two decades ago. Related Stories TV Creative Arts Emmys, Night One: Winners List TV Alan Cumming Lands Third Straight Emmy for Best Reality TV Host Hargitay also spoke about this particular moment in her career, where she’s living by the motto of “I just say yes. I said yes to Broadway and I said yes to hosting the Emmys — when they called me, I thought it was a joke, and then I went, ‘Why not?'” “It’s a year of firsts and a year of saying yes and not limiting myself or not being governed by fear. Like, what would I do if I wasn’t afraid? What if it all works out?” she continued. “I’m in that place right now of going, ‘I’ll figure it out.’ I’m really happy right now.” She also gave a hint at her mindset heading into the main show , admitting, “It’s been a big week, this hosting the Emmys is no joke,” teasing that NBC “undersold it to me” and told her it would just be two days of rehearsal, which was “a lie.” However, she expressed how excited she was to be working with The Late Show with Stephen Colbert writing team on her material and added, “I just can’t believe at this place in my life — my third act is starting and it’s pretty awesome.” THR

title: Mariska Hargitay Wins Two Emmys For ‘My Mom Jayne,’ Thanks Gloria Steinem From Stage
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Emmy Awards Night 1 Winners: The Full List Read the full story By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew Director Matt Dougherty, E.P. Krishnamurti In ‘The Natural State’ – Telluride Film Festival Danny Boyle’s ‘Ink’ Makes Tabloid Headlines At Telluride ‘The Row’ First Look: Oscar Winner Bryan Fogel Documents One Man’s Incredible Solo Row From California To Australia – Telluride Film Festival View All September 5, 2026 7:37pm Mariska Hargitay NBC via Getty Mariska Hargitay is warming up to host the televised Primetime Emmy Awards in the best way imaginable – by winning two Emmys for her documentary My Mom Jayne . The HBO film in which Hargitay explores the life and career of her late mother, the actress Jayne Mansfield, as well as a mystery over Mariska’s biological father, won Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Special. Hargitay also claimed the Emmy for Outstanding Directing for a Documentary/Nonfiction Program. The honors came as the 78 th Annual Primetime Emmy Awards kicked off Saturday night in Los Angeles with what were formerly called the Creative Arts Emmys. The show will continue Sunday evening from the Peacock Theater downtown, leading up to the televised Primetime Emmys on Monday, September 14 (airing on NBC and the Peacock streaming platform). Related Stories News 'Antiques Roadshow' Scores First Emmy Win, Breaking 'Queer Eye' & 'Shark Tank' Hegemony News Octavia Spencer Wins First Emmy, Stops Sir David Attenborough Becoming Oldest Emmy Winner Ever Accepting the award for Documentary or Nonfiction Special, Hargitay acknowledged the feminist icon Gloria Steinem , who died Wednesday at the age of 92. Watch on Deadline “My hero and friend Gloria Steinem recently said, ‘Please tell your own story,’” Hargitay shared. “The most important thing we can do for each other is to know each other through stories. I got to know my mother through telling the story. It’s a gift that’s indescribable.” A young Mariska Hargitay with her mother, Jayne Mansfield. Courtesy of HBO Accepting the trophy for directing, Hargitay commented, “I’m utterly overwhelmed. I just wanted to share with you that it took me a while when I decided to make this film during the pandemic. It took me a while to realize that this was my story to tell. I could direct it.” And she alluded again to Steinem’s counsel to women about “telling your own story,” saying, “I just want that invitation to go out, especially to women. I’m so excited to explore and discover and innovate new ways of telling stories from half of the earth’s population because we don’t hear from you enough. I can’t wait to get to know you.” It’s been an extraordinary year-plus for Hargitay, who is entering the 28 th season as the star of Law & Order: SVU . In addition to premiering My Mom Jayne , she made her Broadway debut in Every Brilliant Thing , and then agreed to take on the challenge of hosting the Primetime Emmy Awards. “Dreaming is actually part of planning,” Hargitay said backstage at the Emmys after her two wins. “I’m at a place in my life where I just say yes, I said yes to Broadway, and I said yes to hosting the Emmys. When they called me, they thought it was a joke. It’s a year of firsts and a year of saying yes. Not limiting myself or not being governed by fear. What if it all works out? That’s the process of art. I’m in that place right now, I’ll figure it out. I’m really happy right now.” In the Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Special category, My Mom Jayne triumphed over John Candy: I Like Me ; Marty, Life Is Short ; Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man! , and Ocean with David Attenborough (the latter film won Outstanding Cinematography for a Nonfiction Program and Outstanding Sound Editing For A Nonfiction Or Reality Program). In the documentary directing category, Hargitay was up against Lawrence Kasdan of Marty, Life Is Short ; Judd Apatow and Michael Bonfiglio of Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man! ; Alexandria Stapelton for Sean Combs: The Reckoning , and Rebecca Miller for Mr. Scorsese . ‘Mr. Scorsese’ director Rebecca with Martin Scorsese Courtesy of Apple TV Miller, however, isn’t going home empty-handed. Her five-part docuseries about legendary filmmaker Martin Scorsese won the marquee category of Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Series. Robert De Niro, Leonardo DiCaprio, Jodie Foster, screenwriters Paul Schrader and Nicholas Pileggi, Spike Lee, and Daniel Day-Lewis (Miller’s husband) are among the luminaries who appear in the series. The annual two-day event — taking place ahead of the Primetime Emmys on Sept. 14 — will see over 100 awards handed out, mostly for below-the-line categories. Statues presented on Saturday include honors for variety programming, reality and documentary/nonfiction. Saturday’s big winners included The Late Show With Stephen Colbert , The Muppet Show , Love on the Spectrum , The Traitors , The Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show Starring Bad Bunny and My Mom Jayne: A Film By Mariska Hargitay , which each took home multiple trophies. title: ‘The Debut’ Review: Julianne Moore And Paul Giamatti Get Big Laughs In Jesse Eisenberg’s Hilarious And Even Sweet Look At Community Theatre – Telluride Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Emmy Awards Night 1 Winners: The Full List Read the full story By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘The Debut’ Review: Julianne Moore And Paul Giamatti Get Big Laughs In Jesse Eisenberg’s Hilarious And Even Sweet Look At Community Theatre – Telluride Film Festival ‘The Liberation’ Review: Carrie Coon, Lily James And Bella Ramsey Soar In Guy Nattiv’s Explosive Cult Thriller – Telluride Film Festival ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Heartbreakingly Great As AIDS-Stricken Star Determined To Play ‘Hamlet’ – Telluride Film Festival View All September 5, 2026 7:02pm 'The Debut' Topic Studios, Fruit Tree At times downright hilarious, at other times so farcical it nearly sails over the top, and at other times quite poignant, Jesse Eisenberg ‘s third time out writing and directing a feature film, The Debut , throws it all at the wall, hits its target most of the time, and serves up a complete delight with go-for-broke perfectly pitched comedic performances from Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti that take the risks and get the laughs, some so rich you will have tears streaming down your face. At one point during an intense Moore rehearsal scene the laughter was so pervasive at today’s World Premiere at the Telluride Film Festival that the audience broke out into sustained and raucous applause. It is well deserved because comedy is an increasingly rare bird on the big screen these days, and this one is an absolute joy to behold in a packed theatre. A24 plans to release it this December and it is a gift for moviegoers no doubt. Set in the world of those community playhouses where the talent is usually very local, but full of enough enthusiasm and theatrical chops to fill the house over three day runs, you might be reminded of other comedies also set in the world of theatre like Mel Brooks’ classic The Producers, Christopher Guests’ deadpan wonderful Waiting For Guffman, or even the lesser known gem, 1980’s Those Lips Those Eyes, but Eisenberg who also gives himself a small song and dance role in this one, finds his own corner of the sky in this sub-genre, not afraid to mix all out farce, sweet but loving moments that never try to mock small town productions, and even some pretty dark detours for Moore’s ever dedicated novice cast member. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Reviews Telluride Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews Reviews Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews Moore plays Mona, an unremarkable New Jersey housewife, basically now walking through life unnoticed even by husband (Patrick Fabian) who just wants her to have dinner ready and drive the kids around. You get the feeling this person is so shy she’s invisible, but that all changes when, after seeing a casting call on the supermarket bulletin board she boldly sets out to audition for a local community production of a musical called Nosy Neighbors. With zero acting experience, Mona has never been on a stage before and here must audition for the role of the building supervisor, Miss Danielle. The part instead goes to ace regional performer Serena Cherry, a star veteran of this Jersey theatre which you can tell by the large poster of her as Evita ( Bernadette Peters in a cameo at the film’s start auditioning with a dynamite vocal), but Mona is the only other person auditioning for the role as it turns out (she actually took ALL the info from the bulletin board) and her rather pathetic rendition of one of the show’s songs is quicky stopped by grizzled veteran director Jerry (Giamatti). But despite her family’s complete indifference to this nascent adventure by Mona, she holds out hope somehow to get the role, and eventually she does when diva Serena suddenly drops out complaining the part is just too small for her. With nowhere else to go on short notice, a desperate Jerry casts her, and then tries to mold her into some kind of acceptable performance. But what happens as the movies progresses is when the inner thespian she never knew existed comes roaring to the forefront for Mona. That is ignited during an aforementioned rehearsal where Jerry tries to get her to think out of the box and improvise a moment where she is only supposed to show up and say “your rent is due”. This results in a wild stretch of attempts by Mona to give life to the line, building to sheer insane obscenities responsible for the film’s R rating. If ever there was an instant classic example of comedy timing and delivery it is what Moore does here. Priceless. Suddenly Mona is reborn as an actress searching for meaning in the role much like a Dustin Hoffman in Tootsie , even to the point of spending nights in a rundown Jersey apartment building to get the feel of what Miss Danielle might be “experiencing” on the job. Mona has gone pure method for a woman who no doubt has never heard of Lee Strasberg and thinks that Stanislavsky is a vegetable in the produce department. If you think Eisenberg is going to stop here, this whole section goes to dark extremes as Mona takes this small acting gig too far and drives Jerry up the wall. Moore, as usual, doesn’t play the stereotype but finds real heart in this overlooked soul who is just hoping to find her moment of triumph, of recognition at a point in her life she rightly feels neglected . Joining this community fits the bill, until it doesn’t, and Eisenberg and Moore know just how far to the edge you can go without losing credibility – or the audience. The Debut never does and Moore finds one of her best roles, a chance to again show her comic abilities, but also to achieve a real measure of authenticity in playing a really bad actress who slowly becomes a fairly decent one, the different gradations demonstrating Moore’s remarkable range in pulling off this challenging balancing act. She is as good as it gets. Similarly, far more toned down though, Giamatti delivers in a role tailor made, his line readings perfection, his mounting frustration a riot, and ultimately his own backstory poignantly touching as he explains how his own theatrical dreams never materialized. This is an actor who nails it every time. There is also a choice supporting cast, many plucked from the lights of Broadway and the Tonys starting with Peters doing a nice version of herself, and such stage stars as K. Todd Freeman as Marty the musical director; Colton Ryan, Bonnie Milligan, Lili Cooper, even stars like Craig Bierko and Danny Burstein in blink-and-you-miss them walk ons. Halle Bailey ( The Little Mermaid) , and Havana Rose Liu are sweet as welcoming friends behind the scenes for Mona. Eisenberg wrote all the Broadway-ish songs with titles like “Girl From 4F, Boy From 46D” and the anthem Mona (and Peters) get to sing with varying results, “The City May Have Chewed Me Up (But It Can’t Spit Me Out)”. I want to hear Moore sing that one at the Oscars! He also created the less-than-stellar, but still likeable show this is all wrapped around, Nosy Neighbors. After building on impressive features, When You Finish Saving The World (also with Moore), and his Oscar nominated script for A Real Pain (which won Kieran Culkin an Academy Award), he is showing more facets of his prodigious abilities behind the lens here, not surprising for a multi-talent who is an actor, playwright, fiction writer, filmmaker and now songwriter too. He manages the changing tone of the comedy with great skill, and with something as bananas (literally) as this sometimes dares to get, that is no small task. Can I already proclaim this as the funniest comedy of the year? There. I just said it. Producers are Emma Stone, Dave McCary, Ali Herting and Eisenberg. title: Alan Cumming Lands Third Straight Emmy for Best Reality TV Host
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kirsten Chuba Plus Icon Kirsten Chuba Events Editor kirstenchuba Follow Sign Up View All September 5, 2026 7:00pm 'The Traitors' Euan Cherry/Peacock Alan Cumming has extended his reign as the ruler of reality TV. Cumming took home the 2026 Emmy for outstanding host for a reality or reality competition program, which was handed out at Saturday’s Creative Arts Emmys ceremony in downtown Los Angeles. The Traitors host was nominated in the category against RuPaul (host of RuPaul’s Drag Race ), Kristen Kish ( Top Chef ), Ariana Madix ( Love Island USA ) and Jeff Probst ( Survivor ). He was not in attendance to accept his award, and presenter Johnny Bananas — a former contestant on The Traitors — took the trophy on his behalf, joking that he wasn’t going to hand over the Emmy “until you bring me back on the show” after he got kicked off early. Related Stories TV Creative Arts Emmys, Night One: Winners List (Updating Live) Movies Telluride Film Fest Kicks Off with Brunch, 'Wild Horse Nine' North American Premiere Cumming has won the category the previous two years, after breaking RuPaul’s eight-year winning streak in 2024; among the group of veteran hosts, Madix is the newcomer to the category, landing her first nom this year as face of Peacock’s mega hit dating show. The Traitors is up for seven Emmys this year, including reality competition program, production design, cinematography, costumes, picture editing and directing, and picked up several wins during Saturday night’s ceremony; the show has 17 total nominations over the course of its history. The Creative Arts Emmys are a two-day affair that see over 100 mostly below-the-line Emmys handed out between the dual ceremonies at the Peacock Theater. These awards are not televised, and take place ahead of the Primetime Emmys show on Sept. 14. The 78th Emmy Awards , hosted by Mariska Hargitay, will air live on NBC and stream on Peacock. THR

title: Octavia Spencer Wins First Emmy
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Emmy Awards Night 1 Winners: The Full List Read the full story By Peter White Peter White Executive Editor, Television @peterzwhite More Stories By Peter ‘Antiques Roadshow’ Scores First Emmy Win, Breaking ‘Queer Eye’ & ‘Shark Tank’ Hegemony Octavia Spencer Wins First Emmy ‘The Late Show With Stephen Colbert’ Scores Emmy Upsets, ‘The Daily Show’s Desi Lydic Also Triumphs View All September 5, 2026 7:00pm Octavia Spencer Amy Sussman/Getty Images Norman Lear remains the oldest Emmy winner after Octavia Spencer scored a surprise win over Sir David Attenborough at the Peacock Theater. Spencer scored her first Emmy in the Outstanding Narrator category for her work on Investigation Discovery ’s true-crime series Lost Women of Alaska . The win prevents 100-year-old Attenborough from becoming the oldest Emmy winner ever. Attenborough, who has been on television screens for over 70 years, had a 40% chance of winning the award given that he was nominated twice in the category for his work on Netflix’s A Gorilla Story: Told By David Attenborough and Nat Geo’s Ocean with David Attenborough. Related Stories Late Night TV 'The Late Show With Stephen Colbert' Scores Emmy Upsets, 'The Daily Show's Desi Lydic Also Triumphs News Jimmy Kimmel Wins Emmy For Second Year In A Row, 'Jeopardy!' Scores Game Show Prize, Again Spencer also beat out an A-list crowd including Jodie Foster, nominated for Netflix’s Breakdown: 1975, and Werner Herzog for Nat Geo’s Ghost Elephants. Watch on Deadline It is her first Emmy, having been previously nominated in 2024 for the same award and in 2020 for Outstanding Lead Actress In A Limited Series or Movie for her role in Self Made: Inspired By The Life of Madam C.J. Walker. Speaking backstage after the win, Spencer said, “Before there was an implosion of true-crime networks, there were people like me who [were] interested. True-crime, these things actually happen. I was a consumer who watched for entertainment. There was something always greater to say if I ever had a platform, I would do something. Lost Women was the perfect vehicle.” Spencer campaigned hard for the award, turning up to plenty of Emmy events. Last month, speaking at Deadline’s Contenders: The Nominees Studio, Spencer said , “I think there are a lot of people who are very new to the true-crime genre. I’m not, I’ve been studying it. I read a horrible story, a true-crime story, when I was 11 and I think it made an indelible mark on me.” A Gorilla Story: Told by David Attenborough (Toby Strong / Silverback Films / Netflix) The shock win means that Lear, who won the Emmy for Outstanding Variety Special (Live) in 2020 as a producer for Live In Front Of A Studio Audience when he was 98, remains the oldest Emmy winner ever. Attenborough will have to be consoled that he is still the oldest nominee in Primetime Emmy history and the oldest person to win a Daytime Emmy for Secret Lives of Orangutans , which won the Outstanding Daytime Personality – Non-Daily award last year when he was 99. ‘The Debut’, ‘The Liberation’, ‘Elsinore’ Reviews; Inside ‘In The Breach’ ‘Primetime’ Hits The Lido; Lee Chang-dong Interview; Oasis Doc; Reviews; More ‘Brand New Day’ Owning Labor Day Frame, Nears ‘Force Awakens’ For U.S. No. 1 Broadway Fall Preview: The Stars Are Coming To New York Read More About: Comments

title: Alanis Morissette Sues Former Tour Manager Over Alleged “Calculated Blackmail Campaign”
full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 5, 2026 6:42pm Alanis Morissette attends the Songwriters Hall of Fame 55th Annual Induction and Awards Gala. Alanis Morissette Alanis Morissette is reportedly suing her former tour manager, alleging that Keren Urinov led a “calculated blackmail campaign” against her, per People . The “Ironic” singer filed the suit on Tuesday, stemming from her working relationship with Urinov in 2025. “Plaintiff Alanis Morissette is the victim of a calculated blackmail campaign orchestrated by a disgruntled former tour manager,” the lawsuit reads, per People . “Morissette will not agree to work with an incompetent blackmailer for the next 15 years or pay her a ransom under the gun.” Related Stories Music Olivia Rodrigo's Inaugural Daisy Chain Fields Draws Massive Crowd to SoCal for a Day of Music and Empowerment Music Alanis Morissette, Ella Langley to Perform at Spotify's SXSW Showcase (Exclusive) According to the documents obtained by the outlet, Morissette’s legal team alleges that Urinov was “flagged for inspection and detained at a U.K. airport” when she was traveling with the singer to Spain. Urinov told Morissette and her team she was arrested and authorities issued a seizure notice, alleging there was marijuana and xylazine in her bag; she showed officials her Israeli medical marijuana license and was released, per People . The suit claims that the tour manager and her own legal team sent Morissette “increasingly extortionate” letters, where she threatened to sue. Urinov allegedly told the seven-time Grammy winner that she could “end to the matter” with a 15-year, full-time employment contract comprised of “an income equivalent to that of a tour director with annual increases and bonuses.” After Morissette did not comply with the “brazen demands,” Urinov and her lawyer allegedly sent her a letter “implying she would accuse Morissette of drug trafficking,” People added. The singer is suing on allegations of civil extortion, fraud and negligent misrepresentation. Morissette was previously embezzled by her former manager Jonathan Todd Schwartz. He admitted to embezzling more than $7 million from Morissette and other celebrity clients in 2017. Schwartz penned an apology essay for The Hollywood Reporter at the time, where he wrote, “To say I am incredibly ashamed and disappointed in myself is an understatement.” THR

title: ‘The Late Show With Stephen Colbert’ Scores Emmy Upsets, ‘The Daily Show’s Desi Lydic Also Triumphs
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Emmy Awards Night 1 Winners: The Full List Read the full story By Peter White Peter White Executive Editor, Television @peterzwhite More Stories By Peter ‘Antiques Roadshow’ Scores First Emmy Win, Breaking ‘Queer Eye’ & ‘Shark Tank’ Hegemony Octavia Spencer Wins First Emmy ‘The Late Show With Stephen Colbert’ Scores Emmy Upsets, ‘The Daily Show’s Desi Lydic Also Triumphs View All September 5, 2026 6:26pm Desi Lydic / Stephen Colbert Getty / CBS The Late Show with Stephen Colbert had an unexpectedly good night at the first evening of the Emmy awards . The canceled series came away with two big upsets at the event formerly known as the Creative Arts Emmys . Colbert Before Air won the Emmy for Outstanding Short Form Comedy, Drama Or Variety Series and and The Late Show won Outstanding Writing For A Variety Series. The latter is a particular surprise given that Last Week Tonight with John Oliver has won that award for ten years in a row, starting in 2016. Also in that category was Jimmy Kimmel Live! Related Stories News Jimmy Kimmel Wins Emmy For Second Year In A Row, 'Jeopardy!' Scores Game Show Prize, Again News Norah O'Donnell Claps Back At Bari Weiss Critics After 'CBS Mornings' Return: "This Is So Silly. Just Watch Our Show" Tom Purcell, executive producer of The Late Show, picked up the award. “I’d like to thank all who those who keep late-night going, [John] Oliver, [Jimmy] Kimmel, super important institution in this country, keep the flame burning, guys,” he said on stage. Watch on Deadline The Colbert Before Air win was also surprising. The digital series, as best one can tell, has only aired ten episodes in the last year, mostly around 2-4 minutes in length. The CBS show also picked up a picture editing win. It bodes well for Colbert’s chances to win the main late-night Emmy on September 14, where he is up against Jimmy Kimmel Live!, The Daily Show , Last Week Tonight and Saturday Night Live. The show was up against last year’s winner The Daily Show: Desi Lydic Foxsplains, Tom Segura’s Netflix comedy Bad Thoughts, The Randy Rainbow Show and SubwayTakes with Kareem Rahma. The latter has particularly campaigned this season and has built huge buzz with the format, which sees celebrities and civilians give hot takes on the New York subway. The Daily Show didn’t go away empty handed, though. Jordan Klepper Fingers The Pulse: Give The Man A Prize won Outstanding Writing for a Nonfiction Program, beating PBS’ The American Revolution and Apple’s The Reluctant Traveler with Eugene Levy. Desi Lydic also won the Emmy for Outstanding Performer in a Short Form Comedy or Drama Series. The Daily Show host beat Randy Rainbow and Big Law’s Kim Estes and it is her second consecutive win in the category, having also won last year. Lydic joked on stage at the Peacock Theater about what winning these awards could mean for her. “I’m so afraid if I keep [winning] these, the White House will nominate me to be their press secretary,” she said. title: Ben McKenzie Says He’d “Be Up for” a ‘The O.C.’ Revival: “It Was a Great Show”
full_text: Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All September 5, 2026 5:53pm From left: Adam Brody, Rachel Bilson, Ben McKenzie and Mischa Barton in 'The O.C.' season three. Courtesy Everett Collection Logo text California, here we come — again… possibly? hopefully? Ben McKenzie is weighing in on whether he’d be interested in returning to The O.C. In a new interview with on KIIS 1065, McKenzie was asked by the host if he would be open to “re-doing” The O.C. by returning as “one of the dads,” referencing Peter Gallagher’s Sandy Cohen role. “I don’t know that there has ever been serious talks, but I’d be up for it, sure,” he responded. “Yeah, I think so, under the right circumstances. It was a great show. We had a great time. I learned a lot. I was so young. We were all young.” Related Stories TV 'Modern Family' Duo Christopher Lloyd, Danny Zuker Land Comedy 'Mammoth' at Fox TV 'Sterling Point' Renewed for Season 2 at Prime Video He added that his 10-year-old child, whom he shares with actress Morena Baccarin and briefly appeared in three episodes of season three, “loved it.” “I now have kids come up to me, teenagers, and they talk about what a fan they are of the show. ‘You weren’t even alive when it came out,’” McKenzie continued. “They watch it with their parents.” The 47-year-old’s comments come after Mischa Barton , who played his on-again, off-again love interest, Marissa Cooper, recently teased that a possible reunion might be coming. During the Fox teen drama’s four-season run from 2003 to 2007 — named one of the best teen dramas of all time by The Hollywood Reporter — McKenzie played Ryan Atwood, a troubled teen from Chino, California, who is taken in by his public defender Sandy and his family. Ryan becomes like a brother to Seth Cohen ( Adam Brody ) and is part of the show’s central group alongside Summer Roberts ( Rachel Bilson ) and Marissa. McKenzie went on to lead the TV series Southland and Gotham following The O.C. He is currently promoting his documentary about the crypto industry, Everyone Is Lying to You for Money . title: Jimmy Kimmel Wins Emmy For Second Year In A Row, ‘Jeopardy!’ Scores Game Show Prize, Again

The comedian has picked up for Outstanding Host for a Game Show for his work on ABC ’s Who Wants To Be A Millionaire . It is his second consecutive win in the category, having scored it for the same show last year. Kimmel beat Celebrity Family Feud’s Steve Harvey, Jeopardy! ’s Ken Jennings, Pop Culture Jeopardy!’s Colin Jost and Match Game’s Martin Short. Apart from Pop Culture Jeopardy! , which moved from Amazon in its first season to Netflix for its second season, the category was dominated by ABC shows. full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Emmy Awards Night 1 Winners: The Full List Read the full story By Pete Hammond , Damon Wise September 4, 2026 1:20pm Clockwise from top left: 'Primetime,' 'Ink,' 'Bunker,' 'The Echo Chamber' and 'Bucking Fastard' A24; Anthony Dickenson; Blue Morning Pictures; Indigo Film; Lena Herzog The 2026 Venice Film Festival got underway on Wednesday, September 2, with Oscar-winning English director Danny Boyle’s Ink — starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce and Claire Foy — kicking off an 83rd edition that includes films starring the likes of Robert Pattinson, Penelope Cruz & Javier Bardem, Jack Huston & Sofia Boutella, Dakota Johnson, John Malkovich & Sam Rockwell, Alicia Vikander & Susan Sarandon, Nick Nolte and Kate & Rooney Mara in their first movie together. Related Stories Festivals Venice Film Festival 2026 Photos: Opening Ceremony, ‘Ink’ Premiere & George Clooney Lifetime Achievement Presentation Festivals Venice Head Talks Studio Absence, Dearth Of Female Golden Lion Contenders & Why Neon Nixed Luca Guadagnino’s ‘Artificial’ – Q&A Along with Ink, this year’s competition lineup includes such buzzy titles seeking awards-season glory as Florian Zeller’s Bunker, Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime , Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love , Andrea Pallaoro’s The Echo Chamber , Casey Affleck’s Company and Warner Herzog’s Bucking Fastard. Studio titles largely are absent this year, but the overall lineup also includes new films by Luca Guadagnino, Paul Schrader and Wim Wenders along with Laura Poitras’ short about ICE protests in Minnesota, and Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace’s doc on the comeback of rock band Oasis. Watch on Deadline Check out Deadline’s reviews out of Venice, and keep checking back as we add more. Click on each headline to read our full review. The Basics of Philosophy ‘The Basics of Philosophy’ Noora Films Section: Out of Competition Director: Paul Schrader Cast: Jack Huston, Sofia Boutella, Daniel Zovalto, Bill Pullman, Dana Delany, Shiloh Fernandez, Karl Glusman, Elizabeth Petruso, Santiago Cabrera, Trevor Dolden, Richard Gere Deadline’s takeaway: With this introspective character study, Schrader continues to making the kind of grownup films we rarely get to see anymore, outside of Europe at least. He never presents easy answers in his movies — same with this deep dive into the philosophy of life and the key question we can ask of many Schrader characters, “Can we change?” — PH Bucking Fastard ‘Bucking Fastard’ Lena Herzog Section: Competition Director-screenwriter: Werner Herzog Cast: Kate Mara, Rooney Mara, Orlando Bloom, Domhnall Gleeson Deadline’s takeaway: Although it appears to start with a tone of gentle mockery, there’s something quite sweet and generous at work beneath the stylized strangeness of the tale of two sisters played by Rooney and Kate Mara, a tone that Werner Herzog has never really struck before in his fiction work, with the possible exception of 2019’s Family Romance LLC . — DW The Girl with the Leica ‘The Girl with the Leica’ Manuel Alberto Claro Section: Orizzonti Director: Alina Marazzi Cast: Emilia Schüle, Aaron Altaras, Luna Wedler, Lucas Englander, Thomas Schubert, Sebastian Schneider, Idan Weiss, Lia von Blarer, Hans-Christian Hegewald, Jeremy Mockridge, Joel Basman Deadline’s takeaway: The jazzed-up, unconventional biopic of the late photojournalist Gerda Taro asks questions about the the fine line between bravery and ego in the process of bringing back dispatches from the front line, but its structure over-complicates a simple yet quite profound meditation on an artist’s identity and legacy. — DW Ink ‘Ink’ Netflix Section: Competition Director: Danny Boyle Cast: Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce, Claire Foy, Jonathan Hyde, Lucy Russell, Abigail Amin, Bertie Carvel, Brian Gleeson, Christopher Fulford, Patrick Kennedy, Blake Harrison, Georgie Henley Deadline’s takeaway: Danny Boyle with his whip-smart, in-your-face stye is the perfect filmmaker to bring this world set in 1969 London to life as the brash if trash visionary Rupert Murdoch and his hand-picked editor-in-chief launch what would become a new era of tabloid journalism, changing the media world for better or worse in the process. Here all the cylinders are firing, and it is thrilling stuff indeed. — PH Wild Horse Nine ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Searchlight Pictures Section: Competition Director: Martin McDonagh Cast: John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell, Steve Buscemi, Mariana di Girolamo, Ailín Salas, Tom Waits, Parker Posey Deadline’s takeaway: John Malkovich gives a career performance in a perfect if unexpected casting. This so-called “buddy movie” of a wildly different stripe easily is one of the year’s best films, and in its own peculiar way the most spiritual.
